ABSTRACT

Voice disorders are one of the incipient symptoms of Parkinson's disease (PD). Most of the existing PD severity prediction methods are based on baseline features, and generally select features with high relevance for dimensionality reduction. To further improve the prediction performance, the LDFSF and GWT-RF-Att methods are proposed respectively from the perspective of feature selection and feature transformation. The LDFSF method utilizes dynamic feature selection strategy based on SOM clustering to select feature subsets with high correlation, low redundancy, and high complementarity from voice features. The GWT-RF-Att method uses graph wavelet transform to extract the more effective feature set based on the baseline features, and uses random forest improved by attention mechanism to improve the prediction performance of the model. The results on the Parkinson's telemonitoring dataset show that the performance of the two methods is better than that of the existing comparison methods, thus verifying their effectiveness.

INTRODUCTION

Parkinson's disease (PD) is a common degenerative nervous system disorder characterized by trembling, slow movement, postural balance disorder, and other motor symptoms. And PD patients will also be accompanied by symptoms such as voice disorders (Xue et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2023a). Fortunately, voice disorders are one of the earliest symptoms of PD, which can generally be observed five years before clinical diagnosis (Zhang et al., 2023b). By analyzing the voice features of subjects, it is possible to use machine learning methods to analyze the severity of the diagnosed patients' conditions, which is of great significance for the early diagnosis and treatment of PD patients.

For the regression tasks for Parkinson's disease, using voice data for severity assessment of PD has shown promising results. The Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS) is an internationally recognized measure for assessing the severity of Parkinson's disease symptoms (Yoon & Gaw, 2021). It consists of two components: motor-UPDRS and total-UPDRS, which assess motor symptoms and overall assessment of PD symptoms. In the past few decades, simple linear regression (LR), nonlinear classification regression tree, k-nearest neighbors (KNN) regression, and support vector regression (SVR) are commonly used traditional prediction methods for Parkinson's disease symptom severity due to their computational efficiency. However, these models may not achieve the desired prediction accuracy (Tsanas et al., 2010). In recent years, machine learning and neural network methods have gained popularity in UPDRS prediction. Mayo & Frank (2017) applied Bayesian regression and its modified version to improve prediction accuracy and generalization ability. Neural networks, such as feed-forward neural networks (Xiang et al., 2016) and adaptive network-based fuzzy inference systems (ANFIS) (Nilashi et al., 2017), have also been employed due to their ability to handle nonlinear relationships. However, neural networks require large datasets and careful parameter tuning, and may be prone to overfitting and lack of generalization ability (Hlavica et al., 2016).

To enhance the generalization ability of the PD severity prediction model, Tunc et al. (2020) proposed a combined approach of feature selection and extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) based on decision trees (DT) to predict UPDRS scores in PD patients. Despotovic et al. (2020) used the automatic relevance determination (ARD) method to rank PD voice feature weights. In the study by Tsanas et al. (2021), random forest (RF), SVR, and XGBoost were used to evaluate PD severity, and RF exhibits superior prediction performance compared to SVR and XGBoost. RF has been found to possess higher effectiveness, stability, and robustness compared to artificial neural networks (Dong et al., 2021), making it a suitable choice for predicting UPDRS scores in PD patients. Furthermore, the selection of different input features for RF can impact the model's prediction performance (Liu et al., 2018).

However, the above method has the following two problems, which may increase the prediction error of the model. On the one hand, while these methods consider the correlation of the feature to the target value, relying solely on the property may be insufficient. The redundancy and complementarity between features are conducive to the selection of feature subsets that can improve the performance of the model. On the other hand, most of the existing methods for predicting the severity of Parkinson's disease are based on baseline features and the RF regressor, but the information of baseline features is limited, and some decision trees in RF have poor prediction results, which may affect the performance of the model.

To address the above two issues, this chapter proposes two methods to address the aforementioned issues in PD research. Firstly, the local dynamic feature selection fusion (LDFSF) method is introduced for feature selection based on relevance, redundancy, and complementarity in PD symptom severity prediction tasks. This method introduces the maximal information coefficient (MIC) as an effective measure of feature relevance (Reshef et al., 2011). To reduce computational complexity, the proposed method utilizes self-organizing map (SOM) (Nilashi et al., 2019) clustering to select features within each cluster. This method also designs a dynamic feature selection (DFS) strategy based on clustering, which can dynamically update the importance between candidate features and the selected feature subset. The selected features are input into the random forest model to predict the disease severity of the patients. The advantage of the LDFSF method is that the feature subset selected by relevance, redundancy, and complementarity is more universal. The experiment evaluation was conducted on the Parkinson's telemonitoring dataset (PTDS) to compare the proposed LDFSF method with the traditional FS method and the existing literature. The results demonstrate that the LDFSF method effectively selects a small subset of features, leading to superior prediction performance when combined with appropriate regressors. Secondly, this chapter proposes the GWT-RF-Att method that combines the graph wavelet transform (GWT) with attention-weighted RF, which extracts a more effective feature representation and achieve better PD severity prediction results. Based on PD voice features, the GWT-RF-Att method extracts effective frequency features by using GWT, and adaptively selects the decision tree model with better performance in random forest for prediction by using the attention-improved random forest model, thus improving the prediction accuracy. Therefore, the advantage of the GWT-RF-Att method in this paper is that more features related to the target values are obtained and the performance of RF in predicting the severity of PD condition is further improved.

The main contributions of this chapter are as follows:

  • (1) From the perspective of feature selection and feature transformation, this chapter proposes the LDFSF and GWT-RF-Att methods to optimize voice features of patients to achieve better PD severity prediction performance.
  • (2) The LDFSF method not only considers the correlation between features and target value, but also designs a dynamic feature selection method based on clustering for analyzing the redundancy between features and the complementarity between features and feature sets.
  • (3) The GWT-RF-Att method transforms the baseline features by GWT to obtain effective features that are more relevant to the target value, and improves the prediction performance by introducing the attention mechanism into random forest.
  • (4) Experiment results on the PTDS dataset show that the proposed LDFSF and GWT-RF-Att methods obtain superior performance in PD severity prediction compared to existing methods, thus validating the effectiveness of optimizing patient voice features from the perspective of feature selection and feature transformation.

RELATED WORKS

Feature Selection

Scholars have proposed various feature selection (FS) methods for the tasks of PD severity prediction. Tunc et al. (2020) utilized the Boruta algorithm to establish feature significance by exploring relationships among all relevant features and analyzed the selected features. They concluded that vocal fold vibration patterns were crucial indicators for assessing PD severity. Tsanas et al. (2021) evaluated the features using four FS algorithms to obtain features with high importance and tested three regression models, namely SVR, XGBoost and RF regressors. The results show that the prediction performance of RF consistently outperformed SVR and XGBoost, which verifies its superiority in PD severity prediction. Despotovic et al. (2020) ranked PD voice feature weights using the ARD method and selected eight features with the high relevance with the target value. Gaussian process can extend multivariate Gaussian distribution to infinite many random variables, which has been successfully used in latent variable modeling of high-dimensional data. By combining ARD with Gaussian process, the number of PD voice features was reduced, and prediction accuracy was improved.

The above FS methods based on relevance and redundancy have analyzed the intrinsic relationships between PD voice features and combined with suitable classifiers and regressors to obtain good prediction models. However, the FS analysis using only these two properties is not sufficient. This is because a single feature with low classification ability may have a high dependency on other features, that is, there is complementarity between features, and adding them to the feature subset may help to enhance the recognition ability of the model (Chen et al., 2021). Therefore, in order to select effective features and improve the accuracy of the prediction model, it is necessary to analyze the relevance, redundancy and complementarity of features at the same time.

Graph Wavelet Transform

The graph wavelet transform is a method that utilizes data to construct a weighted path graph, consisting of vertices and edge weights. These edge weights represent the similarity information between connected vertices. By transforming known data into a graph representation, the GWT enhances the input information (Dong et al., 2021). Prior to the application of GWT, the wavelet transform (WT) is a widely used multi-scale analysis method in signal processing. It decomposes the original sequence into sub-series at different frequency scales, extracting important information from the signal. The wavelet coefficients obtained from WT decomposition provide detailed information about the frequency changes in the sequence. In the context of PD pathological signals, WT is commonly employed to extract the time-frequency characteristics. Utilizing these features, predictive models for PD can be developed, improving accuracy (Chakraborty & Nandy, 2020).

Furthermore, WT can also extract sequence information by decomposing the sequence into coefficient vectors of different scales. By analyzing the relationship between these coefficient vectors and the target value, the impact of different sequences on the target value can be determined. Consequently, WT can extract frequency features from the PD feature vector. Lai et al. (2016) proposed a method using graph wavelet transform, which involved sorting the features in the sequence, extracting sequence information, and generating a new feature vector. The effectiveness of the features extracted by the wavelet transform was subsequently verified.

To effectively represent pathological signals in PD patients, the GWT method is employed in this chapter to extract frequency features from PD feature vectors. However, the PD feature vector is high-dimensional data, and different arrangements of features represent different information of frequency. To address this challenge, the chapter considers different feature arrays.

Prediction Methods: Machine and Deep Learning

Machine learning (ML) algorithms have been widely utilized for PD diagnosis, providing reliable and early detection of the disease (Senturk, 2020). Tsanas et al. (2010) compared the performance of the LR method and classification and regression trees (CART) in mapping PD voice features to UPDRS values. CART outperformed linear predictors, indicating that linear combinations of voice features are not effective for UPDRS prediction. Since then, researchers have proposed more effective prediction models. Ji et al. (2018) and Yoon & Li (2019) combined transfer learning with ML algorithms to account for differences in disease trends among PD patients. Jain & Shetty (2016) found that KNN achieved the lowest error compared to multivariate LR and regression tree methods. Nilashi et al. (2020) utilized SVR with processed PD voice features, both achieving the best performance among the compared methods. XGBoost and RF have also been employed for PD severity estimation. Tunc et al. (2020) utilized the Boruta method to select informative features and fed them into XGBoost, resulting in the lowest mean absolute error. RF, known for its ensemble learning voting mechanism, finds wide application in biomedical informatics (Xu & Pan, 2020). Sharma et al. (2019) and Tsanas et al. (2021) combined RF with their proposed models, all achieving improved prediction results, which highlight the reliability of RF in predicting PD severity and its significant potential.

In addition to ML techniques, deep learning (DL) has gained significant attention due to its powerful automatic feature extraction capabilities (Zhang et al., 2022). In PD classification tasks, Oung et al. (2018) analyzed audio signals using empirical wavelet transform and empirical wavelet packet transform. They employed KNN, probabilistic neural network, and extreme learning machine as classifiers, achieving high classification accuracy. Kadam & Jadhav (2019) proposed a feature ensemble learning method based on sparse autoencoders, verifying its validity and practical value in PD research by comparing it with various classification methods. For predicting symptom severity in PD patients, Xiang et al. (2016) designed a three-layer feedforward neural network structure and utilized a Gaussian mixed regression model for nonlinear prediction, which achieved smoother results compared to KNN and regression tree predictions. Nilashi et al. (2019) developed a method that combined singular value decomposition and adaptive ANFIS to predict disease progression in PD patients. This method improved the time complexity and accuracy of the PD diagnosis system. Nilashi et al. (2020) constructed a prediction model based on a deep belief network and integrated the prediction results using SVR, further enhancing the accuracy of PD severity prediction. However, DL models require careful tuning of hyperparameters to avoid underfitting and overfitting issues (Shahid & Singh, 2020). Moreover, DL models are data-driven and known for their data-consuming nature, requiring larger datasets to demonstrate their excellent performance (Nilashi et al., 2020). In contrast, the Parkinson's telemonitoring dataset is relatively small, which limits the common use of DL methods in PD symptom severity prediction tasks. However, as the PD voice dataset continues to expand, DL methods still hold great potential.

PROPOSED METHOD

Problem Definition

The aim of this chapter is to predict the severity of Parkinson's disease symptoms. Let the PD dataset be D={X,Y}, where Y with dimension M×1 represents the PD severity score of motor-UPDRS or total-UPDRS for M samples. with dimension M×N represents the feature of all samples. xm with dimension N×1 represents the N-dimensional feature vector of the mth sample. One of this chapter of objective is to predict the severity Y of Parkinson's disease patients based on their voice feature vector X. Due to the absence of a straightforward linear relationship between the voice features and the target values (i.e., motor-UPDRS or total-UPDRS), this experiment employs a nonlinear function f(∙)to capture the complex relationship between them. Denoting the true target value as Y and the corresponding predicted value as Y’, then the PD symptom severity estimation problem can be formulated as:

Y’= f(X,Y). (1)

LDFSF Model

In this chapter, the proposed LDFSF method consists of three main components: MIC relevance analysis, DFS strategy based on SOM clustering, and regression model prediction. The detailed process is depicted in Figure 1.

Relevance-Based Feature Selection

The MIC is not limited to specific function types and can capture linear, nonlinear, functional, and non-functional relationships. Among them, functional relationships include linear functional relationships, nonlinear parabolic, periodic, exponential functional relationships, etc., and the superposition of various functions belongs to non-functional relationships. Thus, MIC is an effective method to evaluate the relevance between variables. Given the nonlinear nature of Parkinson's voice data, MIC can be used to effectively measure the relationship between PD voice features and the target value.

Figure 1. Schematic diagram of local dynamic feature selection fusion method

PD dataset can be represented as D={X,Y}, where , represents the feature vector of the sample, N and M represent the feature dimension and the number of samples, respectively. Y = {motor-UPDRS, total-UPDRS} denotes the target value. To begin with, this chapter calculates the MIC score between features and the target value. The main concept of MIC is to divide the scatter diagram grid between the feature variable fi and the target value Y, and then calculate the relevance between variable fi and target value Y in each grid using mutual information. The specific steps are as follows:

Step1: Grid division. Suppose that all the data between PD voice features and the target value in the dataset is a finite set of ordered pairs . MIC aims to identify all the relationships between variables by dividing the value range of feature f into a segments and the value range of target value y into b segments. The grid of a×b is defined as G. The division of the variable space has a significant impact on the MIC results and consequently affects the relevance between features and the target value.

Step 2: Mutual information is calculated after the grid is divided. MIC computes the relevance of variables within each grid using mutual information. The mutual information MI(f,y) represents the degree of association between the feature variable f and the target value y within a specific grid. It is defined as:

(2)

The joint probability distribution function between variables f and y, denoted as p(fk,yk), is approximated by the proportion of samples falling into specific grids. The marginal probability distribution functions of f and y are denoted as p(fk) and p(yk), respectively.

Step3: Calculate the maximum MI. The maximum MI is calculated by varying the number of divisions a and b in grid G, changing the location of divisions in the grid and repeating the calculation of mutual information. The MIC value obtained under different division methods is denoted as MI’ and represents the mutual information value of the grid G. The maximum mutual information formula of D’ under a given grid G is obtained:

MI’(D’,a,b) = max MI(D’|G). (3)

Where D’|G represents different distributions of data D’ for a given grid G.

(5)

Where B(M) refers to the upper limit value of the division within the grid G. The value range of MIC(D’) is [0,1]. The larger the MIC value, the stronger the relevance between f and y, that is, f is a strong relevant feature. The smaller the MIC value indicates that the relevance between f and y is weaker, and the f is more likely to be removed. When MIC=0, f is irrelevant and should be removed.

Dynamic Feature Selection Based on Redundancy and Complementarity

The feature selection methods consider both relevance and redundancy to select the optimal subset of features. However, in some cases, the interaction between highly redundant features and other features may have a positive impact on the model. This chapter proposes an approach to select the optimal feature subset. Firstly, PD voice features with high relevance are clustered using SOM to obtain candidate features from different clusters. Then, features are dynamically selected from the candidate features based on their relevance, redundancy, and complementarity to form the final feature subset. Among them, SOM clustering can divide the candidate features into several clusters, and DFS selects the features of each cluster, which can greatly reduce the number of candidate features and decrease the complexity of the model.

Self-Organizing Mapping Network Clustering

To better approximate the complex relevance between PD multivariate voice features (Chen et al., 2021), this chapter uses SOM to cluster the voice features with high relevance with the target value. Algorithm 1 outlines the process of clustering PD features using SOM. The SOM network comprises an input layer and a competition layer. The input layer represents the feature vectors, while the competition layer consists of dimx×dimy neurons. The relevance between feature vectors and neurons is determined by distance, and neurons are activated through competitive learning. The best matching unit (BMU) is the activated neuron at each moment. The weight vectors of neurons within the BMU's neighborhood are updated based on the learning rate η(t,d). The learning rate η decreases as training time t and topological distance d between neurons and the BMU increase. This process updates the weight vectors of the winning neuron and its neighbors to make them closer to the input vectors, effectively mapping high-dimensional PD voice features onto a low-dimensional space.

After obtaining the weight vector W for each neuron in the output layer, the high-dimensional features are mapped to the two-dimensional plane of the output layer. Clustering is performed by determining the shortest distance between the feature vector and each neuron in the output layer. In this method, the similarity of the input PD voice feature data is expressed through the feature mapping of nearest neighbors in the SOM clustering, while preserving the topology of the data.

Select an input vector fi(t) from X’

d(fi(t)–Wv(t)) = ||fi(t)–Wv(t)||
dis = d(fi(t)–Wv(t))

Dynamic Feature Selection

The dynamic feature selection (DFS) strategy in this section considers both the relevance between features and the target value, as well as the impact of feature redundancy on the importance of candidate features. It can select the those features that are highly relevant, minimally redundant, and exhibit high complementarity. Figure 2 illustrates the process of dynamic feature selection based on SOM clustering.

Figure 2. The dynamic feature selection process based on SOM clustering

The DFS strategy in Figure 2 starts by selecting features with the highest MIC value from each cluster in SOM clustering. These features are then sorted based on relevance and added to the selected subset. To choose features with low redundancy and high complementarity from the cluster, the proposed DFS strategy considers the MIC(f,y) between candidate features f and the target value y, as well as the average redundancy Rf between candidate features and the selected subset Fs. This approach allows for dynamic updating of the complementarity Cf between candidate features and the selected subset. The redundancy between features fi and fj is defined as MIC(fi,fj). A higher value indicates a smaller difference in information among features, indicating a stronger level of redundancy. The average redundancy Rf and complementarity Cf are defined as follows:

(6)

(7)

Where Fs represents the selected feature subset, and |Fs| represents the number of features in the set Fs. Cf combines relevance and redundancy to assess the significance of candidate features and represents the level of complementarity between candidate features and the selected subset. The larger Cf value indicates a stronger degree of complementarity between candidate features and the selected subset.

In the current clustering method, a dynamic feature selection strategy is employed. This strategy calculates the complementarity Cf between each candidate feature f and the selected feature set Fs using Eqs. (6) and (7). The candidate feature set Fc is then sorted in descending order based on the Cf value. The feature f with the highest Cf value is added to the selected feature subset Fs, creating a new set . Both Fs and are input into the RF regressor, and the mean absolute error MAE(Fs) obtained by each is denoted as MAE(Fs) and , respectively. If , the feature f is added to the selected feature subset Fs, and it is removed from the candidate feature set Fc. However, if , the second feature in Fc is added to Fs to determine the error. This process continues until Fc is empty. At this point, all the features in the next cluster are considered as a new candidate subset , and the features with the highest complementarity with the selected feature subset are selected from and added to Fs. The above process is repeated until all candidate features have been tested or the number of features in Fs reaches the predetermined upper limit set by the experiment. In such case, Fs becomes the final output feature subset.

Random Forest Prediction Based on Attention Weighting

After frequency feature extraction of PD feature vectors, the dimensions of the new feature vectors , and are all J+1. RF is a powerful algorithm for handling high-dimensional data and can effectively reduce the risk of overfitting. Therefore, the multi-dimensional feature matrices , and are input into RF to predict the motor-UPDRS and total-UPDRS of PD patients. RF regression is an ensemble learning algorithm that consists of multiple decision regression trees. Each decision tree in RF is trained on a random subset of samples and features. Suppose the feature vectors , and are input into RF to generate T decision trees, then the prediction results of 3T decision trees is , where Trt represents the prediction results of tth decision tree.

RF obtains the final prediction value by averaging the results of all decision trees under the assumption that each decision tree's results are accurate. However, since the input feature vectors , and contain different frequency information and the frequency characteristics of the decision trees are different, the output results of the decision trees will also differ. Due to the randomness of RF, not all decision tree predictions are accurate, and the importance of each decision tree's prediction results may vary. Simply averaging the prediction results of all decision trees may increase the prediction error of RF.

To improve the model performance, attention weights are introduced to the decision trees. Figure 6 illustrates the improved random forest prediction model that incorporates attention weighting. It can adaptively focus on decision trees with higher prediction accuracy and suppress decision trees with poor prediction performance, thereby reducing prediction error. The weight of attention is calculated as follows:

The attention mechanism enhances the predictive impact of key decision trees in RF by assigning distinct weights to each decision tree. The prediction result of the weighted decision trees is Tr’:

EXPERIMENT

Parkinson's Telemonitoring Dataset

The Parkinson's telemonitoring dataset (PTDS) (Tsanas et al., 2010) originates from the University of Oxford and is widely used for predicting the severity of PD symptoms (Ji et al., 2018; Tsanas et al., 2021; Despotovic et al., 2020; Yoon & Li, 2019). The dataset comprises voice data collected from 42 patients with primary PD, including 28 males and 14 females, each with a 5-year medical history. Patients were required to record 6 sustained vowels /a/ with varying loudness levels on the same day every week, without taking medication during the test. This recording process spanned 6 months, resulting in a total of 5,875 voice samples. Tsanas et al. (2010) applied linear and nonlinear voice signal processing algorithms to extract 16 voice features from the recorded data as shown in Table 1. Additionally, sex and age are considered important factors in predicting PD symptom severity and can be used to track UPDRS values (Xue et al., 2023). Motor-UPDRS and total-UPDRS are commonly used to express different degrees of Parkinson's disease, with a range of 0-108 and 0-176, respectively. The higher their value, the more severe the patient's disease. In this study, the maximum motor-UPDRS and total-UPDRS values observed were 55 and 41, respectively. Thus, all subjects included in the study exhibited moderate Parkinson's symptoms. Previous research has demonstrated a linear increase in UPDRS scores over a 5-year period without drug treatment for early-stage PD patients. Therefore, the UPDRS scores of patients were evaluated at the beginning, after 3 months, and after 6 months during data collection. Using piecewise linear interpolation, the UPDRS values at other time points were estimated based on the actual UPDRS scores at these three stages (Tsanas et al., 2010). In summary, this dataset provides valuable information for studying PD symptom severity prediction and includes voice features, sex, age, and UPDRS scores at different time points for PD patients.

Experiment Setup

Experiment Setup of the LDFSF Model

During the experiment, the parameters to be adjusted in the proposed LDFSF method mainly include the determination of grid division mode in MIC and related parameters in SOM. Among them, the number and method of grid division in MIC have a significant impact on the relevance measurement of features. Therefore, this chapter set the upper limit B(M) of grid G division in MIC as M0.6, which has been proven to be the most effective in practical applications (Reshef et al., 2011). The parameters of SOM are set as follows: learning rate η=0.9, output grid size dimx=dimy=4, and maximum number of iterations T=1000. In the process of dynamic feature selection, the training set is used for feature selection, the validation set is used to evaluate the quality of the selected feature subset, and the test set is used to assess the performance of the prediction model that combines the feature selection framework with the regressor.

To assess the model's ability to predict the severity of PD symptoms and validate the accuracy of the prediction results, this chapter employs mean absolute error (MAE) as the evaluation metric for the prediction model. MAE is calculated as follows:

(20)

Where M’ represents the number of test samples, yk and represent the true value and the predicted value of the model, respectively. The smaller the MAE, the closer the predicted value is to the true value, indicating better prediction performance.

Experiment Setup of the GWT-RF-Att Model

To simplify the modeling process, this chapter utilized the standardized K-means algorithm to cluster similar samples in the Parkinson's telemonitoring dataset. The choice of the number of clusters can impact the performance of the clustering algorithm. A previous study (Nilashi et al., 2019) explored the number of clusters for this dataset and suggested that 4 or 9 clusters would be reasonable. However, considering the relatively small size of the PD dataset, we opted for 4 clusters.

The GWT-RF-Att model employs the GWT method to extract different frequency features from PD feature vectors. The GWT involves two main parameters: the number of wavelet decomposition layers and the selection of wavelet basis. The accuracy of vector decomposition results can be determined by the number of wavelet decomposition layers, which can be chosen by analyzing the length of the PD feature vector. In this case, the length was set to 2 due to its short length. Additionally, a suitable wavelet function needs to be selected for wavelet analysis. The Daubechies (db) wavelet is commonly used due to its orthogonality and satisfaction of Parseval's theorem. Therefore, this chapter selected the popular “db2” wavelet basis.

To improve the performance of the GWT-RF-Att model, the hyperparameters of the attention-weighted RF model were optimized. This includes the number of decision trees in the RF, units in the attention layer, units in the FC layer, and the training batch. The best parameter selection method is adjusting only the relevant parameters while keeping others constant to achieve the best prediction performance (Zhang et al., 2021). The best hyperparameters for predicting motor-UPDRS and total-UPDRS in each cluster are provided in Tables 2 and 3, respectively.

Experiment Results

Experiment Results of the LDFSF Model

Result of the Selected Feature Set

In this chapter, the proposed LDFSF method is employed to address the regression problems associated with PD diagnosis. By selecting the optimal subset of features and combining them with suitable regressors, the LDFSF framework effectively achieves accurate PD severity prediction. The effectiveness of RF methods on public dataset PTDS has been previously demonstrated. Therefore, this chapter integrates the LDFSF framework with RF to validate the feasibility and reliability of the proposed method.

For PD severity prediction, the LDFSF method initially assesses the relevance between features and the target value using the MIC, as depicted in Figure 7. Features with low relevance to the target value (UPDRS) can degrade the performance of the classification and regression models. To address this, the chapter sorts the MIC(f,y) values of all features in descending order and eliminates the bottom 20% of features with low relevance, retaining the top 80% of features. Subsequently, the SOM method is employed to cluster the selected features. The clustering results of SOM on features are presented in Table 4, revealing high similarity within each cluster and the potential presence of redundant features.

Figure 7. Relevance (MIC) between features and the target value UPDRS

The proposed dynamic feature selection process, combining SOM clustering with RF, derives the optimal feature subset based on redundancy and complementarity. Figure 8 illustrates the accuracy and MAE variation of the validation set during the dynamic feature selection process. Existing FS methods using the same PTDS dataset typically yield the simplest feature sets of 8. To compare with the latest literature, the proposed DFS strategy limits the number of selected features to 8 for PTDS dataset. As shown in Table 4 and Figure 8, the DFS strategy stops running in cluster 3 when the number of selected feature sets reaches 8.

Effect of SOM Clustering

Table 5 presents the performance of the proposed LDFSF model, both before and after incorporating SOM clustering, along with the corresponding time consumption. This analysis aims to highlight the impact of SOM clustering on the prediction model.

As shown in Table 5, the prediction model's running time is reduced on both datasets after SOM clustering. This can be attributed to the high similarity of features within the same cluster and the low similarity between clusters. The proposed method focuses on the relationship between candidate features within the same cluster and feature subsets during dynamic feature selection, avoiding the consideration of irrelevant features in other clusters, thus reducing the computational cost of the model. For the prediction results, the performance of the model after SOM clustering is improved in both classification and regression prediction, which is consistent with the results of Nilashi et al. (2019) and Nilashi et al. (2020). This outcome may be attributed to SOM clustering's ability to identify feature relevance, and dynamic feature selection methods that incorporate redundancy and complementarity can better analyze the intrinsic connections between features. Specifically, SOM clustering groups features based on similarity, and the high similarity within each cluster suggests potential redundancy. For example, as shown in Table 4, cluster 3 contains features with high inter-feature relevance (Despotovic et al., 2020). Since they measure voice signals similarly, some redundant features may need to be eliminated. However, the dynamic feature selection method based on SOM clustering not only reduces computational costs but also helps remove redundant features, thereby enhancing the prediction performance of PD regression models.

Performance Comparison With Existing Methods

In order to further validate the effectiveness of the proposed LDFSF framework and its combination with RF for prediction, this section compares the LDFSF method with traditional FS methods and recent literature results.

Table 6 presents a comparison of the effects of traditional FS methods and the LDFSF method on model performance. The traditional FS methods, such as ReliefF, mRMR, and Boruta (Tunc et al., 2020), select features based on relevance to the target value and redundancy between features. The LDFSF framework in this chapter adds complementarity to this foundation to explore the intrinsic connections between features. To verify the effectiveness of combining relevance, redundancy, and complementarity for feature selection, Table 6 compares the performance impact of different feature selection algorithms on the prediction model using the same regressor. RF performs well in PD regression prediction (Tsanas et al., 2021). Therefore, in Table 6, each feature selection method is combined with RF to compare the performance of the FS method. Additionally, the same number of features is set in this section to compare the effectiveness of the selected feature subsets. In summary, this section provides a comprehensive comparison of different feature selection methods, highlighting the effectiveness of the proposed LDFSF framework combined with RF for prediction.

Table 6 demonstrates that the proposed LDFSF method outperforms traditional FS algorithms in PD severity progression prediction tasks. ReliefF only considers feature relevance, while mRMR and Boruta focus on selecting features with high relevance and low redundancy. However, these methods do not consider the complementarity between candidate features and feature subsets. In contrast, the LDFSF method combines relevance, redundancy, and complementarity for feature selection, resulting in the proposed prediction model shows superiority with the same regressor RF in Table 6. Specifically, the MAE of motor-UPDRS predicted by the LDFSF method is 10.00%, 8.99% and 10.99% lower than that of ReliefF, mRMR and Boruta respectively, and the MAE of total-UPDRS predicted is 6.13%, 6.13% and 9.13% lower than that of ReliefF, mRMR and Boruta respectively.

Furthermore, Table 7 compares the results of the proposed LDFSF method with those of existing literature. Specifically, this chapter compare the results of Ji et al. (2018), Yoon & Li (2019), Tsanas et al. (2021), and Despotovic et al. (2020) with the results of the proposed LDFSF method on the PTDS dataset.

Table 7 reveals that the LDFSF model achieves better prediction results compared to the literature. For regression, Ji et al. (2018) and Yoon & Li (2019) utilize transfer learning to address the limited data issue in PD patients, but face challenges in measuring similarity across different time dimensions. Tsanas et al. (2021) employ four FS methods combined with RF for PD severity assessment, but potential bandwidth restrictions or transmission errors may affect accuracy. Despotovic et al. (2020) achieve better prediction results with the Gaussian process regression model based on ARD, but ARD does not consider redundancy and complementarity when ARD calculates the weights of individual features and selects the feature with higher weight to form a feature subset. In comparison of Table 7, the LDFSF method surpasses the proposed method by Despotovic et al. (2020) in terms of prediction performance, validating the effectiveness of feature selection based on relevance, redundancy, and complementarity. Overall, the LDFSF method enables the selection of a small yet effective subset of PD voice features, providing certain reference value for accurate PD severity assessment. However, the rough extraction of traditional voice features from the whole voice data makes the model accuracy limited.

Experiment Results of the Proposed GWT-RF-Att Model

Effectiveness of GWT

To provide further insight into the effectiveness of the GWT proposed features, the Spearman correlation coefficient is calculated to quantify the correlation between the features and UPDRS (Tsanas et al., 2021). Figure 9 displays the Spearman correlation coefficients between PD baseline voice features and UPDRS, as well as between frequency features and UPDRS.

The strength of the correlation between each feature and UPDRS is indicated by the absolute value of Spearman's correlation coefficient. In Figure 9, the deeper the red or blue color, the stronger the correlation between the corresponding feature and UPDRS. It can be observed that compared to the baseline PD features, the frequency features extracted by GWT exhibit a significantly higher number of features with a high Spearman correlation coefficient with UPDRS, confirming the effectiveness of these frequency features.

Figure 9a. Spearman correlation coefficient between features and UPDRS in cluster1
Figure 9b. Spearman correlation coefficient between features and UPDRS in cluster2
Figure 9c. Spearman correlation coefficient between features and UPDRS in cluster3
Figure 9d. Spearman correlation coefficient between features and UPDRS in cluster4

Figure 9 also reveals that some features extracted by GWT have a weak association with UPDRS. The original RF model averages the results of all decision trees, assuming that each tree is accurate. However, if a decision tree selects a large number of features with little correlation with UPDRS, it may reduce prediction performance. By employing an attention layer to adaptively learn and assign different attention weights to the decision trees generated by RF, the model can focus more on decision trees with better prediction performance. Therefore, the RF model improved by the attention mechanism may build a more accurate prediction model.

Clustering Results

To validate the clustering results, Figure 10 displays the MAE for each cluster. Tsanas et al. (2021) pointed out that when the MAE of the PD severity prediction model is less than 5 points, this prediction model will be very useful in practice. The bar chart in Figure 10 demonstrates that after dividing the Parkinson's telemonitoring dataset into four clusters, the MAE of the proposed GWT-RF-Att model for the prediction of motor-UPDRS and total-UPDRS are all less than 5, which indicates the practicability of this model.

Figure 10. Performance results for PD progression assessment in each cluster

The UPDRS consists of three main parts: “Mentation, Behavior and Mood,” “Activities of Daily Living,” and “Motor Examination.” The motor-UPDRS is specific to assessing motor signs of Parkinson's disease, including voice features. On the other hand, the total-UPDRS incorporates not only motor-UPDRS but also mental health and daily activities. Therefore, it is assumed that motor-UPDRS is more closely related to voice disorders in sound-generated motor activities compared to total-UPDRS (Despotovic et al., 2020). This explains the lower MAE of predicted motor-UPDRS in each cluster compared to total-UPDRS, as depicted in Figure 10.

The statistical significance of GWT features is assessed using the p-values, as presented in Table 8. The p-value is determined through t-tests to evaluate the significance of the method. It is observed that in all cases, the GWT features exhibit a statistically significant correlation with UPDRS (p-value < 0.05) (Tsanas et al., 2021). Consequently, the GWT features obtained in this chapter are deemed statistically significant.

Comparison of Results

To evaluate the performance of our proposed GWT-RF-Att model, we compared it with traditional machine learning methods and state-of-the-art methods from the literature. Baseline methods including SVR, XGBoost, and RF were used in the experiment. Additionally, we compared our proposed method with GWT combined with SVR, XGBoost, and RF (i.e. GWT-SVR, GWT-XGBoost, GWT-RF) to highlight the influence of GWT-extracted features, and with RF combined with attention mechanism (RF-Att) to assess the impact of attention weights on prediction results. To ensure fairness, all models were trained and tested on the same datasets with optimized parameters.

Table 9 presents the MAE of motor-UPDRS and total-UPDRS predicted by the aforementioned models on the test set. The results indicate that replacing baseline features with GWT-extracted features improves the prediction performance of traditional methods, and the addition of attention weighting reduces the MAE of RF. Furthermore, we compared our proposed model with several advanced methods from the literature, including FDAMF, PTL, FS-RF, and GPR-ARD. The performance of these methods on the same Parkinson's telemonitoring dataset is also reported in Table 9.

The specific prediction results of each model in Table 9 can be analyzed as follows. Among traditional machine learning methods, both XGBoost and RF outperform the single prediction model SVR due to their integrated algorithms. Moreover, RF combines bagging and random feature selection, effectively addressing the overfitting issue observed in XGBoost. This not only enhances the robustness of the RF model but also improves its prediction accuracy. Consequently, compared to SVR and XGBoost models, RF demonstrates a reduction in MAE of 40.07% and 40.79% for motor-UPDRS and total-UPDRS, respectively, affirming its effectiveness in predicting PD severity progression. Additionally, compared to SVR, XGBoost, and RF, GWT-SVR, GWT-XGBoost, and GWT-RF models achieve reductions in MAE of 5.05%, 0.58%, 1.18%, and 5.67%, 11.48%, 0.48% for motor-UPDRS and total-UPDRS, respectively. Figure 11 compares the effects of attention mechanisms on the model. It can be seen that the errors are reduced after the addition of attention mechanism. Furthermore, the MAE of motor-UPDRS and total-UPDRS predicted by the GWT-RF and RF-Att models was reduced by 1.18%, 1.78% and 0.48% and 2.39%, respectively, compared to the RF model. Therefore, these results demonstrate that GWT can extract more effective PD features, and the attention-weighting-based RF can focus on the decision trees with better prediction performance. By combining these two methods, the proposed GWT-RF-Att model further reduces the MAE and improves the prediction performance.

Figure 11. Attention weighted RF predicts the MAE for motor-UPDRS and total-UPDRS

Moreover, Table 9 reveals that the proposed model outperforms the existing literature in terms of predicting PD severity, achieving the lowest MAE values. The results show that the MAE of the proposed method for predicting motor-UPDRS and total-UPDRS are 1.53 and 1.91, respectively. The proposed method achieved a significant improvement compared to the best results of the literature in Table 9. The MAE was reduced by 7.27% and 4.05%. In previous studies, methods like FDAMF (Ji et al., 2018) and PTL (Yoon & Li, 2019) attempted to predict the UPDRS score of PD patients by learning from the information of other patients. However, it was challenging to measure the similarity of PD patients in different time dimensions, which limited the reduction of prediction errors. FS-RF (Tsanas et al., 2021) and GPR-ARD (Despotovic et al., 2020) used feature selection algorithms to select important PD features, which improved prediction accuracy. However, this approach may result in the loss of crucial information, affecting the performance of the model. In contrast, the proposed GWT-RF-Att model overcomes these limitations. It utilizes graph wavelet transform to capture more effective PD features and employs an attention weighting mechanism to focus on decision tree models with different prediction performance. As a result, the proposed model effectively enhances the prediction accuracy. Compared with the results of LDFSF method in Table 7, the prediction error of GWT-RF-Att method is lower, which indicates the effectiveness of the features extracted by GWT-RF-Att method. However, since the method requires wavelet transform and attention layer training, the limitation of the proposed model is that the running time of the model may be long.

CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORKS

This chapter proposes LDFSF and GWT-RF-Att methods for PD severity prediction from the perspectives of feature selection and feature transformation, both of which improve prediction performance. The LDFSF method analyzes the relevance, redundancy, and complementarity among PD voice features. It utilizes the maximal information coefficient to determine feature relevance and selects feature subsets with high relevance, low redundancy, and high complementarity using a dynamic feature selection method based on SOM clustering. The GWT-RF-Att method is based on graph wavelet transform and attention weighted random forest. It predicts the severity of current symptoms in PD patients using effective frequency features extracted from PD voice features. This method adaptively focuses on decision tree models with better performance in the random forest for prediction, resulting in improved accuracy. Experimental results on real public PTDS dataset show that both LDFSF and GWT-RF-Att methods have achieved better predictive performance compared to existing methods, thus verifying the effectiveness of these two methods in PD severity prediction.

In future research, combining the two proposed methods to achieve better results is an interesting attempt. Additionally, the causal feature selection method will be introduced to uncover the Markov boundary of the target variable UPDRS. This approach aims to identify voice features that have a causal relationship with UPDRS, thereby enhancing the robustness and practicality of the diagnostic model.

ABSTRACT

The Durban University of Technology is now engaged in a project to create a data lake house system for a Training Authority in the South African Government sector. This system is crucial for improving the monitoring and evaluation capacities of the training authority and ensuring efficient service delivery. Ensuring the high quality of data being fed into the lakehouse is crucial, since low data quality negatively impacts the effectiveness of the lakehouse system. This chapter examines quality control methods for ingestion-layer pipelines in order to present a framework for ensuring data quality. The metrics taken into account for assessing data quality were completeness, accuracy, integrity, correctness, and timeliness. The efficiency of the framework was assessed by effectively implementing it on a sample semi-structured dataset. Suggestions for future development including enhancing by integrating data from a wider range of sources and providing triggers for incremental data intake.

INTRODUCTION

In South Africa, Sector Education and Training Authorities (SETAs) are government-established entities responsible for managing skills development and training in various sectors of the economy. These entities are referred to as Government-Sector Training Authorities (GTAs), and they play a crucial role in the country's efforts to improve skills and training across many sectors. The Durban University of Technology (DUT) has partnered with a South African Government Technical Agency (GTA) to enhance the data management strategy used by the GTA for an ongoing project. This is achieved by assisting DUT students in developing supplementary talents. In order to enhance the data management capabilities of the GTA, it was recognized that a comprehensive system was required to store data and generate reports automatically. Following the discussion, the DUT team suggested using Microsoft Azure services to establish a data warehousing solution. Additional context for the project is presented by (Mthembu et al. 2024). This chapter focuses on establishing a Data Lakehouse for a Training Authority in the South African Government sector. One crucial aspect is investigating techniques to ensure the integrity of data as it moves through the system, particularly during the Incremental Extract-Load-Transform Pipelines at the Ingestion Layer employing Data Orchestration.

In the age of Big Data, where the vast amount of information poses both advantages and challenges, effectively handling and using data has become essential for organizational success. The wide range of data types, including structured, semi-structured, and unstructured forms, requires a sophisticated approach for data manipulation (Azad et al., 2020). The Extract, Load, Transform (ELT) framework is a versatile tool that is well acknowledged for its efficacy in negotiating the complexities of contemporary data settings (Singhal & Aggarwal, 2022). However, as data pipelines get larger and more complicated, guaranteeing the integrity of data quality (DQ) has become more important.

The emergence of big data has necessitated the use of Distributed Data Warehouses (DLH). Harby and Zulkernine (2022) suggested that the big data age has brought up new issues for traditional Data Warehouses (DWs). The increase in diverse data quantities caused by digital transformation presents a difficulty for traditional data warehouse solutions in businesses (Čuš & Golec, 2022; Giebler et al., 2021). Furthermore, (Barika et al. 2019) highlight the challenges faced by researchers in organizing, controlling, and implementing big data workflows, which differ significantly from typical workflows. After undergoing transformation and being placed into the data warehouse (DW), the original filtered information is no longer retained (Figueira, 2018). According to Conventional, (Nambiar and Mundra 2022), the ETL procedure is deemed inadequate for fulfilling certain data management requirements.

A Data Lake (DL) is a comprehensive storage and exploration system specifically intended to manage large amounts of varied data. It has been widely recognized as the preferred method for processing and storing various data (Begoli et al., 2021).An further research undertaken by the DUT team emphasizes the significance of data governance in establishing authority over data utilization and decision-making via the implementation of processes, rules, organizational structures, and responsibilities (Mthembu et al., 2024).Failure to regularly maintain a data lake might result in expensive and difficult data management. Insufficient execution of data governance in DL systems may result in the creation of a chaotic “Data Swamp,” which undermines the worth of information in knowledge management and analytical systems owing to the presence of difficult-to-process and analyze data.

DLH emerged as an innovative concept that integrates the benefits of DL and DW, enabling companies to efficiently handle, analyze, and store vast quantities of data in a versatile and cost-efficient way. According to (Harby and Zulkernine 2022), this is intended to expedite the process of extracting information effectively.

The objective of this chapter is to provide a structured system for managing and incorporating data into a Data Lakehouse (DLH) to guarantee the accuracy and reliability of the data. The research outlines the following goals, which are aligned with the aim:

  • • Analyze current literature to identify crucial parameters and quality control measures for data orchestration and intake.
  • • Create and implement a framework that incorporates the essential elements and quality control measures indicated for efficiently managing and integrating data in a distributed ledger healthcare (DLH) system.
  • • To assess the efficacy of the established framework and provide suggestions for data quality management in the orchestration and ingestion of data for a distributed ledger technology (DLT) healthcare system.

By offering further study data on the use of Azure Data Factory (ADF) for the orchestration and ingestion of data into a data lake it enhances the existing knowledge base to facilitate future study in data orchestration and ingestion using Azure Services. Identify the limitations of establishing a pipeline for data orchestration and ingestion. Furthermore, offering comments for prospective investigations in this domain enhances the importance of our study. The study explores the concept of data orchestration, which is a crucial area that combines data management and quality control. The main objective is to provide quality control procedures in incremental ELT pipelines inside the Ingestion Layer of a Data Warehouse (DW). The research highlights the difficulties associated with using semi-structured data and recognizes the need for specific approaches to guarantee optimal data quality and integrity. The study result describes the creation of a pipeline and framework that allows data from SharePoint to be imported into a specific container inside the data lake architecture. The pipeline includes essential steps for converting semi-structured data into a structured format and utilizes data orchestration methods to ensure the correctness, completeness, and consistency of the data being processed.

Section 1 clearly explains the cause of the gap and offers a strong remedy, which is shown by the objectives and driven by the desire to provide valuable insights to the field of study and achieve specific research outcomes. The explicit references to the study's aims, scope, and delimitations provide a comprehensive understanding of the content and boundaries of this research. The methodology, datasets, matrices, and tools and platforms to be used in the experiment are described in Section 2. This provides sufficient time for thorough preparation for the subsequent Chapter Four. Section 3 demonstrates the results of the experiment and assesses the efficacy of the created artifacts. In addition, Section 3 discusses the constraints and offers an evaluation of the experiment's execution. Section 4 presents the findings of the experiments and evaluates the overall performance of the manufactured artifacts, in line with the experimental aspect of the study.

LITERATURE REVIEW

(Figueira, 2018) posits that the primary objective of the area of big data is to provide a means of managing vast quantities of data in order to generate valuable insights and knowledge. (Gupta, 2023) explains that the concept of big data originated from the three main factors known as the 3V's. These factors include: volume, which refers to the amount of data available (Liu & Zhang, 2020; Pratsri & Nilsook, 2020); variety, which encompasses a wide range of data types and sources, such as structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data (Liu & Zhang, 2020); and velocity, which represents the speed at which new data is generated and transferred (Liu & Zhang, 2020). Subsequently, the 5V's framework emerged, including the original 3V's and incorporating the following additions: The veracity of Big Data is of utmost importance, as ensuring accurate data without duplication is a challenging and time-consuming task. Value refers to data that is valuable and holds significance for business applications, including analysis for summarization and strategic planning, with the aim of enhancing product value and improving competitiveness in the target market. Figure 1, created by Sandhu in 2021, illustrates many instances of the 5V's.

Figure 1. Representation of the 5V’s

The three categories of content format sources are structured data, semi-structured data, and unstructured data. Structured data pertains to data that is systematically organized in a certain hierarchical pattern. Storing data in this manner facilitates search engines in presenting and comprehending it more effortlessly. Semi-structured data is characterized by an irregular and implicit structure, without a clearly defined data model. In this particular database format, the distinction between data and schema is not readily apparent. In contrast to organized data, unstructured data functions as its complete opposite. The absence of a well-defined framework results in the processing of data being a time-consuming task.

Semi-structured data presents the most difficulty in handling due to its lack of adherence to a pre-established data model and absence of a stable schema. This is a result of its irregular and implicit framework (Dickson & Asagba, 2020). (Nadal et al. 2022) have identified factors that make the ingestion of semi-structured data into a pipeline with schema flexibility challenging presenting difficulties in creating a standardized framework for processing since it may be necessary to accept various data examples.

(Raj, et al. 2020) asserts that ETL and ELT are the primary classifications of data pipelines. Data lakes (DLs) use the Extract, Load, and Transform (ELT) methodology, in which the first step involves loading the “raw data” followed by its subsequent transformation (Cherradi & El Haddadi, 2022).The ELT technique, in contrast to the ETL procedure, follows a similar fundamental idea but differs in terms of sequencing. Instead of doing the transformation before loading, the data is loaded first and then converted afterwards. Data orchestration has a wider range of activities compared to data integration. While data integration mainly concentrates on consolidating data for reporting purposes, data orchestration includes tasks such as resource allocation, monitoring, data discovery, preparation, and integration, processing, and linking enriched data across various landscapes (Dinh & Nguyen, 2022). (Kevin and Ginger 2021) highlight the objective of the system to efficiently handle and combine data, consequently improving or establishing corporate operations.

Data intake is usually the first layer in the design. The primary function of the intake layer is to acquire data from various sources and integrate it into the distributed learning system. (Cherradi & El Haddadi, 2022) have shown that data intake at the ingestion layer may be performed in several ways, depending on the source and destination. These methods include batch processing, real-time processing, or a combination of both. According to (Isah et al. 2019), stream processing involves the handling of continuous or dynamic data, in contrast to batch processing. Stream processing, a technique that allows for real-time data analysis without relying on persistent storage, plays a crucial role in social media platforms such as Twitter and Facebook. The velocity at which data is received greatly impacts this process (Nambiar & Mundra, 2022). Stream processing excels at handling large amounts of data that is constantly flowing at high speeds, and it can be quickly expanded to accommodate increased demands (Hlupić & Puniš, 2021). (Nambiar and Mundra, 2022) provide a hybrid processing strategy that combines batch and stream processing methods. This approach aims to achieve higher accuracy while minimizing processing time.

The chosen DQ qualities are correctness, validity, data integrity, accuracy, completeness, and timeliness. Although the threshold conditions were met, it was considered unnecessary to evaluate consistency for ingestion-layer processes. Consistency guarantees the consistent presentation of data, its alignment with other data, and its freedom from contradiction. This was considered more relevant to source systems and transformation-oriented pipelines. Assessing the comprehensibility of data is primarily important for systems-level governance, rather than being a central concern at the data input layer.

Performing a data integrity check during data import is essential for preserving data dependability and preventing data corruption throughout the transfer process between providers and repositories (Anastasova & Yanev, 2021), assesses whether data values adhere to predetermined criteria, and any variation suggests possible issues in the process of collecting the data. According to (Peng et al. 2015), data validity pertains to the integrity of data, namely its consistency and correctness throughout its existence. Data accuracy refers to the extent to which information precisely and faithfully portrays its intended topic or process (Anastasova & Yanev, 2021). Completeness refers to the state of data including all the anticipated properties and linked instances, which determines the extent of information (Koltay, 2020).Timeliness refers to the age of the data and is of utmost importance in industrial systems that handle continuous production. Any delays or gaps in the data might lead to inaccurate management choices. (Gabarro and Stewart, 2021) emphasize that the effectiveness of an orchestration's dependability may be assessed using two separate measures. Firstly, by examining its behavioral comprehensiveness measured by the number of its calculated results.

Collection of Data

The provided dataset is a CSV file that includes personnel information sourced from datablist.com. The collection includes User ID, First Name, Last Name, Date of Birth, and Job Title for 100 entries. Only the first 80 recordings will be subjected to ingestion for the purpose of this experiment. The following 20 records are allocated for testing data import after the first phase. The data entries are delimited by semi-colons, and these delimiters will be eliminated when converting the CSV file to a SQL database table. It is crucial to recognize that the first row of the CSV denotes the column headings.

Process of Dataflow

Figure 4 depicts the flow of data from the source, which is represented by SharePoint. The dataset being transferred is represented as a CSV file, which contains semi-structured data. Arrows symbolize the conduit that will be used for the transmission of the data. Significantly, Azure Data Factory will be used for this procedure. The data will be transported from the source to the DL and then duplicated in a container known as “Raw”. The data contained inside this container will stay in its original, unaltered state, prohibiting any modifications to be made. Data timestamp is used to monitor new instances, indicating the current status of the data. Subsequently, the data residing in the Raw container will be replicated and transformed into a table inside an Azure SQL database, facilitating the implementation of data orchestration. Two more columns will be included, namely hashing and date timestamp. Hashing generates a distinct hash value that serves as a unique identifier for a record, hence preventing record duplication. The date timestamp will record the precise moment that the data was either added or changed. Subsequently, the organized information will be placed in the data lake inside a container referred to as “Curated”. However, this study will specifically examine the functionality of data orchestration for curate data. Data orchestration will be used to prevent the duplication of previously added records. This will reduce data duplication caused by hashing. If there are any modifications to the data of an existing record, it will be updated. Furthermore, to enable the gradual intake of data, a trigger mechanism will be deployed to automatically execute the pipeline at certain intervals.

Computation of Metrics

The term “reference dataset” in this study refers to the anticipated quantity of records that should be included in the dataset (Mahanti, 2019). The expected number of records refers to the anticipated number of records, whereas the actual number of records is the outcome obtained after doing the experiment. Frequently, a “benchmark” dataset is used as a reference for comparison. This benchmark is considered to provide a full and accurate depiction of the topic under consideration. The benchmark is a projection of the anticipated quantity of records used to assess the comprehensiveness of the dataset in issue.

Wholeness

Completeness pertains to the degree to which the whole of the anticipated records is acquired. The completeness of the dataset is assessed by calculating the ratio between the actual number of records and the total anticipated number of records. The completeness result might be represented either as a percentage or as N/A. The success criteria for the result are 100%.

The following illustrates the meaning of the symbols in the equation:

Correctness

Data correctness pertains to the absolute lack of mistakes; it adheres to a binary idea where data is classified as either accurate or incorrect, with no middle ground. Accuracy may vary, but for data to be considered accurate, it must mostly be right. Correctness refers to the absolute adherence to truth and accuracy in data, whereas accuracy quantifies the extent to which the data accurately reflects the world it represents. However, in order for any data to be acknowledged as accurate, its fundamental accuracy is indisputable. The measure of accuracy is represented by either a “Yes” or “No” or “Not Applicable”. The success criteria for the result are zero.

The following illustrates the meaning of the symbols in the equation: Corr: the degree of data completeness. Arecords: the aggregate count of factual entries included in the dataset. Validity and Integrity

Validity refers to the accuracy and soundness of information, whereas integrity refers to the consistency and reliability of data.

A record would be considered legitimate if the hashing is accurate. Essentially, this is the total number of legitimate records among the total number of records that were consumed. Timeliness

Timeliness, in the context of data management, pertains to the velocity at which data is provided or made available to business users. Essentially, it measures the time difference between the instant data is generated and when it is shown to the user. The “Occurrence Time” is a vital component of timeliness since it precisely identifies the specific instant when a real-world event, represented by the data, occurred. It also represents the moment when a certain characteristic or value associated with an object first became tangible. Essentially, “Occurrence Time” denotes the first time. In order to quantify this, the duration of data transmission is determined by calculating the difference between the end time and the start time, which is expressed in seconds. The success criteria for the result must be achieved within a time frame of 120 seconds. Significantly, several programs provide information on the length of the execution.

The following depicts what the symbols represent in the equation:

  • • Time(s): The rate of time it takes to ingest the dataset in seconds.
  • • ST: The Start Time (Occurrence time) of the dataset.

  • •

    ET: The End Time (Data delivery time) of the dataset.

    Time(s) = ET – ST (6)

If:

Time(s) < 120s; then valid

Time(s) > 120s; then not valid.
