Framework for Managing and Coordinating Data

Figure 6 represents the structure that will facilitate the assessment of data orchestration. Prior to anything else, it is important to finish the scenario instances. In the subsequent stage, it is necessary to document the beginning count of rows, the procedure, and the specific specifics of the conclusion in the test case. After completing the previous procedures, the following step is to execute the pipeline and finally record the outcomes in the test case and assess the overall result of the experiment.

Figure 6. Data Orchestration Framework

Procedure for establishing the pipeline using Azure services:

  • Step 1: You need to establish an Azure account.

In order to access the Azure portal and make use of Azure Services, it is necessary to register an Azure account. Moreover, the utilization of certain services necessitates the acquisition of credits, which incur charges commensurate with the nature of the services generated and used.

Step 2: Establishing the environment Begin by creating a resource group to serve as storage for all the resources that will be used. It is important to pick the resource group that will be used for future purposes, if it is relevant. This resource group should be the one that has been formed. To proceed, the subsequent action involves establishing a storage account to securely retain the source data. After a successful deployment, proceed to establish a container. Then, inside that container, create a folder and upload the necessary files into it. Blob storage was used for testing reasons. Subsequently, establish an Azure SQL Server for the purpose of storing the Azure Database. This study employs SQL authentication as the chosen technique of authentication. Users are required to log in with a password in order to access the contents of the database server. Subsequently, proceed to establish an Azure SQL Database. This location functions as the destination where the semi-structured data, in the form of a CSV file, is converted into structured data and then saved in a table. Building a database incurs costs, but building the database server does not. The configuration of the database is determined by the desired performance and intended use of the database. The cost summary will compute the monthly expenses by considering the chosen database configurations. After creating the database, the Azure Data Factory (ADF) instance is created. Once the deployment is finished, the ADF studio may be launched.

  • Step 3: Transfer the contents of a CSV file to a database table.

Create connected services for both the source and sink in ADF. Establish a link service for blob storage, where the CSV file is saved as a blob for the purpose of this study. The second service that is connected is an Azure SQL Database, which is linked to the database. Next, build a new pipeline and choose the dataflow activity. A new data flow has to be generated and assigned as the data flow for the data flow activity. Subsequently, generate datasets for each of the associated services. Subsequently, create a new pipeline and opt for the copy action. Assign the source to the dataset containing the CSV file, and assign the sink to the dataset containing the SQL database. Choose the option to automatically build a table if the table does not already exist in the database. Subsequently, verify the pipeline and troubleshoot any issues.

  • Step 4: Establishing the data orchestration pipeline

Generate a novel data flow, thereafter establish a fresh pipeline, and use the data flow activity. Subsequently, establish the data flow to match the previously generated data flow. Establish two sources: the first source will retrieve data from the blob storage, while the reference source will get data from the database. These sources will be compared. Activating the data flow debug is necessary since it enables the data flow to execute. Generate Link a derived column transformation to the initial source and generate a column for hashing and another for the date timestamp. Given the introduction of two more columns, it is necessary to establish new columns in the database. It is important to note that the data types of the column, the expression returned in the “Dataflow expression builder,” and the database must be the same. Subsequently, it is necessary to establish a connection with a Lookup transformation in order to validate if the records already exist or are considered new. To do this, you may configure the lookup stream to match the reference source. The lookup condition is used to provide the criteria for comparing the two sources with each other. In order to ascertain the outcome of the record after comparison, a conditional split transformation was linked to the dataflow. This study encompasses three potential streams: new record, update, and no action. The state of each stream is determined in its respective condition “Dataflow expression builder”. The process will follow its respective stream and finally reach the sink, depending on the condition that is satisfied. The fresh record stream is linked to the sink, but the update stream needs an extra transformation in comparison. In order to enable record updates, it is necessary to attach an alter row transformation to the update stream. Finally, the sink determines the target dataset where the records will be stored. The update technique varies between the new record stream and the update stream in terms of the selected choices. In the new record stream, only the insert option is chosen, whereas in the update stream, both the insert and update options are selected. Subsequently, the columns in the data flow must be accurately linked to the corresponding columns in the destination dataset.

  • Step 5: Implement the pipeline

To start the pipeline, choose the pipeline built thereafter, and verify the pipeline for any potential errors. Assuming there are no issues, execute the pipeline by choosing the debug option. To see the count of rows written, choose the output option and then pick the data flow details.

Assessment of Framework

Before acquiring and using the ADF environment, this research used a theoretical strategy to execute the experiment and evaluate the efficacy of the generated artifacts. This theoretical assessment included both favorable and unfavorable outcomes for each given situation. The same possibilities were assessed both theoretically and practically.

Assessment of Outcomes

Scenario 1 assessed the initial data import process by absorbing a total of 80 records. Significantly, the reference dataset did not include any previous entries. The newly imported records were cross-referenced with the reference dataset to see whether any records already existed (this process was applied to all scenarios). In addition, the records that are ingested would be assigned a date timestamp and undergo hashing to ensure data integrity. Unfortunately, the data timestamp was not visible. Consequently, a total of 80 records were successfully processed, aligning with the anticipated result. The measures of completeness, accuracy, and validity/integrity achieved a perfect score of 100%, while correctness received a score of 0 (Y). Thus, Scenario 1 was deemed successful.

Scenario 2 was used to evaluate the intake of new records. This was achieved by consuming 10 new records. It is worth mentioning that there are a total of 80 entries included in the reference dataset. Consequently, a total of 10 records were successfully swallowed, aligning with the projected outcome of 90 records being eaten. The metrics of completeness, accuracy, and validity/integrity achieved a perfect score of 100%, however correctness received a score of 0 (Y). Thus, Scenario 2 achieved success.

Scenario 3 included the modification of preexisting records.15 new records were tested, with 10 being new and 5 being pre-existing. The success requirements include the absence of any newly ingested data and the updating of five existing records. The completeness and accuracy achieved a score of 100%, while the validity/integrity achieved a score of 95%. However, correctness received a score of 0 (Y).The compromise of validity and integrity implies a problem in the constructed pipeline, since the preservation of data quality is crucial in a real-world context. An error in the data might render a company's system unreliable and could result in financial consequences. Upon examination, the new records were included, but no records were modified. Consequently, a grand total of 100 recordings were swallowed. Consequently, Scenario 3 did not provide the desired outcome.

Scenario 4 included testing the intake of pre-existing records. The initial amount of records ingested was 100, and 10 pre-existing records were used to test this situation. The anticipated outcome did not need the consumption of any documents. The measures of completeness, accuracy, and validity/integrity achieved a perfect score of 100%, while correctness received a score of 0 (Y). Thus, Scenario 4 achieved its objective.

Figure 7 depicts the time it takes for the pipeline to execute and provide outcomes. The pipeline execution did not beyond 120 seconds, indicating that all scenarios resulted in good results. Scenario 3 took the longest time to finish the experiment and provide results. This scenario included the process of entering and modifying data. Significantly, with every iteration of the pipeline, the execution time decreased. However, because the first run of Scenario 3 was successful, this particular duration was recorded.

General Performance

Upon completion of the experiment, the statistical analysis reveals that the total success rate of 84% surpasses the failure rate of 16% by a ratio of 5 to 1 (84:16 = 5.25:1 ⇒ 5:1). Based on the statistics, this resulted in a favorable outcome. Nevertheless, according to the specifications of data quality (DQ), accuracy is a necessary condition. Consequently, this experiment is considered unsuccessful since the pipeline was unable to update records. Obstacles

The primary obstacle encountered during the actual execution of the experiment was acquiring the necessary credit to access and exploit resources inside the Azure environment. The credit balance imposed limitations on resource creation, namely on the creation of additional “SQL Databases”. In addition, it is necessary to watch the Azure credits while constructing the data flow, since running the debug process incurs costs that depend on the duration of its use. The update stream failed to operate as anticipated, resulting in data that cannot be relied upon. Efforts were undertaken to solve this puzzle; but, the intended result was not achieved. This discrepancy may be attributed to a mismatch in the hashing process. If none of the requirements were satisfied, no records will be impacted. In addition, the date timestamp was successfully implemented in the query editor of the “Azure SQL Database”. However, the pipeline failed to incorporate a datetime stamp for the ingested entries.

CONCLUSION

The aims of this study were accomplished by identifying crucial criteria and implementing data quality control measures based on available literature. Multiple DQ traits were found, prompting a further in-depth investigation of their occurrence and importance. The DQ features used for this study were specifically intended to guarantee the data's quality throughout the process of intake. After successfully achieving the initial study objective, the discovered data quality criteria were employed as measurements in the design and development of the framework for data orchestration and ingestion. The efficacy of the established framework was assessed by implementing the data orchestration and watching the results of the experiment. Therefore, the final research aim has been accomplished. The efficacy of the created frameworks was first assessed in a theoretical manner and then validated via actual evaluation. Theoretical assessment alone would not have completely corresponded to real-world situations; nonetheless, it did contribute to comprehending the outcomes of using the DQ framework, both in terms of success and failure. To fully understand the efficiency of the study's artifacts, it was necessary to practically apply the pipeline. The experiment's practical execution revealed that the assessment of timeliness should be based on the anticipated quality that would be consumed. The figures given in Section 3 indicate that the experiment was successful, with a success rate of 84% and a failure rate of 16%. Despite the positive outcomes, this experiment is considered a failure based on the criteria of DQ. In order to achieve a Defects Quantification (DQ), it was necessary for the experiment to provide a success rate of 100%. The artifacts produced in this research demonstrated a certain level of efficacy, while the findings indicate that they need more refinement to fully capitalize on their potential and enhance their efficiency. Significantly, another crucial outcome of this investigation included the acquisition curves. It facilitated comprehension and firsthand experience of the intricacies involved in designing and executing pipelines, as well as comprehending the functioning of data orchestration. Utilizing cloud technology incurs significant expenses. The primary constraint of this study is the restricted availability of loans. The economic implications of debugging led to a reduction in the experimentation of data orchestration components. Nevertheless, despite the constraints of this study, it has enhanced the comprehension of DQ maintenance and data orchestration. By presenting a comprehensive set of principles for the design and execution of data orchestration systems, it significantly enhances the current knowledge base. Furthermore, it provides valuable insights for the creation of a data orchestration pipeline. Future research should further investigate the adaptation of data transfer between SharePoint and DL, using the analytical framework and empirical insights offered by this study. Additionally, it would be intriguing to ascertain if the findings of this investigation will yield similar outcomes on other cloud platforms such as Amazon Web Services and Oracle. Future endeavors should prioritize the integration of the study's discoveries with deep learning techniques and improving the process of extracting data from SharePoint. Further study is advised to give priority to the creation of a robust framework for managing metadata activities. Moreover, it is essential to provide a trigger function to enable the gradual intake of data from the source. Conducting thorough testing is crucial to determine the efficiency of the framework in data orchestration. Significantly, future research should specifically target the deficiencies found in this study. This involves efforts to enhance the DQ metrics, test case, and address issues related to data updates. Furthermore, it was determined that there is a need to investigate a more efficient approach for first transferring data from the source to the sink. This technique should only prioritize importing the schema utilized from the source to the sink, since the approach employed just copied the entries without confirming the presence of any duplication. Future work should also include the preservation of updated records in a DLH, without overwriting them, in order to retain a comprehensive historical record. Instead, new entries should be introduced and clearly indicated as a distinct version of the current record. The data timestamp might be used in the future for the development of this solution. According to Table 1, the trait of correctness was recognized as one of the DQ attributes mentioned in the literature. Hence, future study should investigate an additional DQ characteristic. Furthermore, it is crucial to prioritize the analysis of different types of changes in future endeavors, since there is a potential for a multitude of changes to transpire throughout time. It is important to take into account the concept of progressively changing dimensions. Finally, there are still many aspects to be improved and taken into account, since this study just scratches the surface of the potential of data orchestration. Hence, future study should delve into more complex aspects of data manipulation within this domain.

KEY TERMS AND DEFINITIONS

Data Ingestion: The process of collecting and importing information from a variety of sources into an archive, e.g. the Data Lakehouse, so that it can be made available for analysis.

Data Lakehouse: A unified data management architecture that enables organizations to store and analyze structured and unstructured data on a single platform, combining the benefits of Data Lakes and Data Warehouses.

Data Orchestration: This is to ensure efficient data flows and integration into a system, often facilitated through automated working processes, by coordinating and managing different processing tasks.

Data Quality: The degree to which data are accurate, complete, timely, and consistent, providing reliable and meaningful information for decision making.

Semi-Structured Data: Data which has an irregular and implicit structure that lacks a defined data model.

Chapter 5

  • Yi Xu
    Anhui University, China

ABSTRACT

Granular computing focuses on structured thinking and problem solving, which solves complex problem based on granular structure. Existing studies on granular structures mainly focus on multilevel granular structure and multiview granular structure respectively, without combining multilevel granular structure and multiview granular structure. In order to describe and solve problem in a more effectively and reasonably way, we propose partition order product space by combining multilevel granular structure with multiview granular structure. To obtain a solution for problem solving in partition order product space, we propose two search algorithms: depth-first searching algorithm and breadth-first searching algorithm. From the viewpoint of granular computing, existing three-way decisions cannot effectively combine multiview and multilevel to make decisions. As the partition order product space follows the principles of multiview and multilevel, we discuss three-way decisions based on partition order product space. We propose four multiview sequential three-way decisions.

INTRODUCTION

Zadeh proposed and discussed the concept of fuzzy information granularity, which was the first time the concept of “granularity” was proposed (Zadeh, 1979). Hobbs published a paper directly titled “Granularity” (Hobbs, 1985), discussing the decomposition and merging of granules, and proposing methods and models for generating granules of different granularities. Lin T.Y. proposed “Granular Computing” during a visit in the University of California, Berkeley (Lin, 1998). Granular computing focuses on structured thinking and problem solving, which are viewed as human-inspired paradigms of computing and information processing (Bargiela & Pedrycz, 2008; Pedrycz, Skowron, & Kreinovich, 2008; Yao, 2009; Yao, 2016). It solves complex problem based on granular structure. In granular structure, a set of attributes (features) is often selected as a view to describe objects from a particular angle. In each view, objects can be further described from different levels of granularities (abstraction), and each granularity determines a level. Multiview and multilevel are two basic principles of granular computing (Yao, 2009; Yao, 2016). In real applications, to achieve a more comprehensive and reasonable solution in problem solving, people usually simultaneously solve a problem from both multiple views and multiple levels rather than just solving a problem from either multiple views or multiple levels (Bargiela & Pedrycz, 2008; Yao, 2009; Yao, 2016). We select medical diagnosis as an example to illustrate the importance of combining multiple views and multiple levels. In medical diagnosis, assume that a doctor needs to diagnose whether a patient has influenza or pneumonia. To obtain accurate diagnostic conclusions, patients usually have to undergo several kinds of examinations, such as routine examinations, including assessments of a patient’s temperature, cough and sore throat; biochemical examinations, including routine blood tests, C-reactive protein tests and mycoplasma pneumonia tests; and imaging examinations, including X-ray, CT and MRI. Different kinds of examinations provide information about patients from different horizontal perspectives, and each kind of examination can be described as a view. In each view, with an increase in the number of examination items, information about patients becomes increasingly detailed, which constructs multiple levels of information and provides information about patients from different vertical perspectives. First, if a doctor gives the diagnosis conclusion only from a single view, such as routine examinations, there is a great possibility of misdiagnosis. Therefore, to make an accurate diagnosis, the doctor usually makes a decision from multiple views. Second, in a view such as imaging examinations, a patient does not complete all examination items at one time, after which the doctor makes a conclusion. Instead, the patient may first implement an X-ray, and then the doctor tries to make a diagnosis. If a diagnosis cannot be reached, the patient may further implement CT. Namely, in each view, doctors usually make decisions from multiple levels step by step. Last, with multiple views and multiple levels of each view, according to the real needs of the patient, he or she can flexibly implement examinations of different views and different levels. For example, the patient may first undergo examinations to assess temperature, cough and routine blood tests. If the diagnosis conclusion cannot be reached from these examination results, then the patient may undergo an X-ray examination and a C-reactive protein test. The doctor usually simultaneously combines the examination results of multiview and multilevel and flexibly chooses different views and different levels in a view to obtain more reasonable decision results.

The existing studies on granular structures mainly focus on multilevel granular structure and multiview granular structure respectively, without combining multilevel granular structure and multiview granular structure. Granular structure based on multilevel is composed of a linearly ordered family of levels, which only provides one view with multiple levels. Granular structure based on multiview provides multiple views, but each view only consists of one level. In order to understand and describe problem in a more comprehensive way, and then solve the problem more effectively and reasonably, given a universe, we take partition as the granulation method. Combining multilevel granular structure with multiview granular structure, we propose partition order product space. Partition order product space is a new granular computing model that simultaneously follows the principles of multiple views and multiple levels. Based on the partition order product space, we can solve a problem from multiple views and at multiple levels in each view. Linearly ordered multiple levels are utilized to represent a view. A partition order product space is the Cartesian product of many linearly ordered levels, which is a lattice. Each node of the lattice is a solution of problem solving, which is a family of one-level views. To obtain a solution for problem solving in partition order product space, we propose two search algorithms, which are referred to as the depth-first searching algorithm and breadth-first searching algorithm.

The theory of three-way decisions proposed by Yao (Yao, 2011; Yao, 2010) can be motivated, interpreted and implemented from the viewpoint of granular computing (Bargiela & Pedrycz, 2008; Fang, Gao, & Yao, 2020; Pedrycz, Skowron, & Kreinovich, 2008; Yao, 2013), which is associated with concept learning (Zhi, Qi, Qian, & Wei, 2019), decision making (Li, Zhang, Zhou, & Huang, 2017; Liang & Liu, 2016; Luo, Hu, & Qin, 2020; Yao, 2019; Zhang, Li, & Liang, 2020), classification (Dai, Zhou, Li, & Liu, 2019; Liu, Li, & Liang, 2014; Savchenko, 2016; Yue, Chen, Miao, & Fujita, 2020; Zhang, Xia, & Wang, 2017) and clustering (Wang & Yao, 2018; Xie, Xia, Wang, & Gao, 2023). In real applications, this theory has been successfully applied in many fields, such as image processing (Li, Zhang, Huang, & Zhou, 2016; Savchenko, 2019), text processing (Zhang, 2019; Behzadidoost, Mahan, & Izadkhah, 2024), recommender systems (Zhang & Min, 2016), data mining and knowledge acquisition (Chen, Li, Min, Liu, & Tsang, 2017; Min, Zhang, Zhai, & Shen, 2020; Wang, Shi, Yang, & Mi, 2019; Wei, Liu, Qi, & Qian, 2020; Xu, Miao, Zhang, & Zhang, 2017). Different from the traditional two-way decisions that must culminate in an immediate decision, when the available information is insufficient or the evidence is not strong enough to support an acceptance or a rejection at a particular level of granularity, the third option of non-commitment allows us to defer a decision to the next level of granularity. From the viewpoint of granular computing, there are mainly four kinds of three-way decisions: classical three-way decisions (Yao, 2011; Yao, 2010), sequential three-way decisions (Yao, 2013; Yang, Li, Liu, Chen, & Luo, 2017; Yang, Li, Fujita,Liu, & Yao, 2017), multigranulation three-way decisions (Qian, Zhang, Sang, & Liang, 2014; Qian, Liang, & Lin, 2017; Sang, Liang, & Qian, 2015; Zhou & Yao, 2010) and multigranulation sequential three-way decisions (Qian, Liu, & Yue, 2019; Qian, Liu, & Miao, 2020). Classical three-way decisions and multigranulation three-way decisions are single-step decisions. Sequential three-way decisions and multigranulation sequential three-way decisions are multi-step decisions. Classical three-way decisions are based on a single view with a single level. Sequential three-way decisions are based on a single view with multiple levels (Yao, 2013; Yang, Li, Liu, Chen, & Luo, 2017; Yang, Li, Fujita, Liu, & Yao, 2017). Multigranulation three-way decisions are based on multiple views, and each view has only a single level (Qian, Zhang, Sang, & Liang, 2014; Qian, Liang, & Lin, 2017; Sang, Liang, & Qian, 2015; Zhou & Yao, 2010). Multigranulation sequential three-way decisions are based on multiple views; each view has a single level and the sequential process is formed using a sequence of thresholds (Qian, Liu, & Yue, 2019; Qian, Liu, & Miao, 2020). In summary, sequential three-way decisions only consider multiple levels and do not adequately consider the issue of multiple views. Multigranulation three-way decisions and multigranulation sequential three-way decisions only consider multiple views and do not sufficiently consider the issue of multiple levels. Sequential three-way decisions, multigranulation three-way decisions and multigranulation sequential three-way decisions separately use multiple views or multiple levels. A relative separation of multiple views and multiple levels calls for their integration. Therefore, we discuss three-way decisions based on partition order product space. Combining depth-first and breadth-first searching algorithms with optimistic and pessimistic fusion strategies, we propose four multiview sequential three-way decisions: depth-first optimistic multiview sequential three-way decisions, depth-first pessimistic multiview sequential three-way decisions, breadthfirst optimistic multiview sequential three-way decisions, and breadth-first pessimistic multiview sequential three-way decisions. The proposed four multiview sequential three-way decisions can make decisions not only from multiview but also at multilevel. Existing three-way decisions can be considered special cases of the proposed models.

We introduce partition order product space in Section 2. In Section 3, we propose two types of search algorithms: depth-first searching algorithm and breadth-first searching algorithm, to obtain a solution for problem solving in partition order product space. In Section 4, combining depth-first and breadth-first searching algorithms with optimistic and pessimistic fusion strategies, we propose four multiview sequential three-way decisions. Section 5 is Conclusion.

PARTITION ORDER PRODUCT SPACE

Partition order product space solves a problem from multiple views and at multiple levels in each view (Xu & Yao, 2019), which simultaneously follows the principles of multiple views and multiple levels. Based on the partition order product space, we can more comprehensively understand and describe the problem and then more effectively and reasonably solve the problem. Given a universe, first, partition order product space uses a partition on the universe to define a level. Second, a nested sequence of partitions is employed to define a hierarchy, which represents a view with a linearly ordered relation. Last, given many views that determine many linearly ordered relations, a partition order product space is proposed based on the Cartesian product of multiple linearly ordered relations, which is a lattice. Each node of the lattice is a solution of problem solving, which is a family of one-level views. The descriptions of important notations are presented in Table 1.

A view is defined by a partition order. A partition order can be constructed by a nested sequence of equivalence relations. There are many methods (Catanzariti, Chiaselotti, Infusino, & Marino, 2020; Chen, Li, Min, Liu, & Tsang, 2017; Liu, Zhang, Ciucci, Wu, & Min, 2018). Theorem 1 indicates that a nested sequence of attribute sets determines a nested sequence of equivalence relations, based on which we can construct a view. In this view, the number of attributes increases with the levels. From the high level to the low level, the quality of granules ranges from coarse to fine, and the size of granules ranges from large to small. Consequently, at a higher level of granularity, one may have a more abstract and compact representation of a decision problem by omitting details, leading to a faster decision process but a less accurate result. On the other hand, at a lower level of granularity, one may have a more concrete and elaborate representation, leading to a slower decision process but a more accurate result.

Theorem 2 indicates that a multi-scale sequence of attribute value sets determines a nested sequence of equivalence relations, based on which we can construct a view. In this view, the scale of attribute value sets increases with the levels. From the high level to the low level, the quality of granules ranges from coarse to fine, and the size of granules ranges from large to small.

A single view provides multilevel understanding and representation of the reality or a problem from a particular angle, and many views produce multiview with multilevel understanding and representation of the reality or a problem. The partition order product space is defined as follows:

The detailed proof is presented in (Xu & Yao, 2019). From Definition 3 and Theorem 3, we discover that POPSm is based on the Cartesian product of m views and that different views provide an understanding and description of a problem from different perspectives. Each view understands and describes a problem from multiple levels of granularity. Therefore, partition order product space provides a multiview and multilevel understanding and description of a problem.

In partition order product space, each node is defined as a problem solving level, which is a family of one-level views.

SEARCH APPROACH

Given a partition order product space POPSm= (×Pi,≼P) determined by m views vi, where each view has ni levels. Based on Definition 3, POPSm has problem solving levels. When we solve a problem, how to search in the partition order product space to find suitable problem solving levels is a crucial problem.

As the topology structure of the partition order product space is a lattice, usually, there are two search strategies. The first search strategy is the depth-first searching strategy, and the second search strategy is the breadth-first searching strategy. In the following part, we give two search algorithms in partition order product space, which are referred to as the depth-first searching algorithm and breadth-first searching algorithm, as shown in Algorithm 1 and Algorithm 2.

In Algorithm 1 and Algorithm 2, according to the depth-first searching strategy and breadth-first searching strategy, we can obtain a sequence of problem solving levels. Based on the sequence of problem solving levels, we can solve a problem from coarse granularity to fine granularity.

In Algorithm 1, steps 3-5 initialize the visited matrix of k problem solving levels as False. Steps 6-14 initialize the adjacency matrix of k problem solving levels. If problem solving level i and problem solving level j are adjacent, adj[k][k] is True; otherwise, it is False. Steps 15-19 traverse problem solving levels in the partition order product space from the current problem solving level l using the depth-first searching strategy. Steps 21-32 is the depth-first traversal function using the recursive method. In this function, first, the unvisited problem solving level l is visited and added to the traversal sequence L and then recursively visits the unvisited adjacent vertices of l. Note that steps 24-26 indicate that if l is the finest problem solving level then the algorithm ends. Usually, the depth-first traversal method traverses all problem solving levels in partition order product space. However, in Algorithm 1, when the finest problem solving level is visited, there is no need to traverse other coarser problem solving levels.

The time complexity of steps 3-5 is O(k). The time complexity of steps 6-14 is O(k2). For function DFS with steps 21-32, which traverses problem solving levels in partition order product space from problem solving levels l and where the time complexity is O(k2), so the time complexity of steps 15-19 is O(k2). In summary, the time complexity of Algorithm 1 is O(k2).

In Algorithm 2, steps 3-5 initialize the visited matrix of k problem solving levels as False. Steps 6-14 initialize the adjacency matrix of k problem solving levels. If problem solving level i and problem solving level j are adjacent, adj[i][j] is True; otherwise, it is False. Steps 16-32 traverse problem solving levels in the partition order product space from the current problem solving level l using the breadth-first searching strategy, which is based on a queue. First, the unvisited problem solving level l is visited and added to the traversal sequence L; it is put into the queue. When the queue is not empty, the head of queue l is dequeued and visits the unvisited adjacent vertices of l; the visited adjacent vertex is put in the queue.

The time complexity of steps 3-5 is O(k). The time complexity of steps 6-14 is O(k2). The time complexity of steps 16-32 is O(k2). In summary, the time complexity of Algorithm 2 is O(k2).

Note that the traversal sequence L of problem solving levels based on the depth-first searching algorithm is different from that based on the breadth-first searching algorithm. We illustrate their difference by an example.

THREE-WAY DECISION BASED ON PARTITION ORDER PRODUCTION SPACE

Three-way decisions are generated from decision-theoretic rough sets (DTRS), which divide the universe into three pair-wise disjoint regions with two thresholds based on the minimum expected overall decision risk (Yao, 2010). From the viewpoint of granular computing, there are mainly four kinds of three-way decisions: classical three-way decisions, sequential three-way decisions, multigranulation three-way decisions and multigranulation sequential three-way decisions.

To clearly illustrate the relationships and differences among these four models, we analyze them from two aspects: the first aspect is their problem description space, and the second aspect is their problem solving space. As classical three-way decisions use one set of attributes to describe objects and there are no multiple levels, the problem description space of classical three-way decisions has only one view, which has only one level. Accordingly, based on the single view and single level problem description space, the problem solving space of classical three-way decisions has only one solution (Yao, 2011; Yao, 2010). The problem description space and problem solving space of classical three-way decisions are shown in Fig.4 (a). As sequential three-way decisions use one set of attributes to describe objects and based on the attribute set to construct multiple levels, its problem description space has one view with multiple levels. Accordingly, based on the single view and multiple levels problem description space, the problem solving space of sequential three-way decisions has multiple solutions and makes decisions from coarse-granularity to fine-granularity constituting a sequential process (Yao, 2013; Yang, Li, Liu, Chen, & Luo, 2017; Yang, Li, Fujita, Liu, & Yao, 2017). The problem description space and problem solving space of sequential three-way decisions are shown in Fig.4 (b). Multigranulation three-way decisions use multiple sets of attributes to describe objects, and there are no multiple levels in each attribute set, so its problem description space has multiple views, but each view only consists of one level. Accordingly, based on multiple views and single level problem description space, multigranulation three-way decisions make decisions by fusing the decision results of multiple views, so its problem solving space has one solution (Qian, Zhang, Sang, & Liang, 2014; Qian, Liang, & Lin, 2017; Sang, Liang, & Qian, 2015; Zhou & Yao, 2010). The problem description space and problem solving space of multigranulation three-way decisions are shown in Fig.4 (c). Multigranulation sequential three-way decisions use multiple sets of attributes to describe objects, and there are also no multiple levels in each attribute set, so its problem description space has multiple views, and each view has only one level. The problem description space of multigranulation sequential three-way decisions is the same as that of multigranulation three-way decisions. However, their problem solving spaces are different. Note that multigranulation sequential three-way decisions use a sequence of thresholds to realize the sequential process instead of constructing multiple levels based on the attribute set. Therefore, the problem solving space of multigranulation sequential three-way decisions has multiple solutions and makes decisions from coarse-granularity to fine-granularity by a sequence of thresholds; each solution is a fusion of the decision results of multiple views (Qian, Liu, & Yue, 2019; Qian, Liu, & Miao, 2020). The problem description space and problem solving space of multigranulation sequential three-way decisions are shown in Fig.4 (d).

Figure 4. Problem description space and problem solving space of different three-way decisions

From the above analysis, classical three-way decisions, sequential three-way decisions, and multigranulation three-way decisions do not combine multiple views and multiple levels. Although multigranulation sequential three-way decisions consider multiple views and multiple levels, they only use multiple views to describe objects, but each view still has only one level, that is, the granularity in each view is fixed and unchanged from coarse-granularity to fine-granularity with the sequential process of decision making. Therefore, we discuss three-way decisions based on partition order product space.

Through depth-first or breadth-first searching algorithms, we can obtain a sequence of problem solving levels in partition order product space. Based on a sequence of problem solving levels, we can make sequential decisions. However, as each problem solving level is a family of one-level views, we need to fuse multiple views at the problem solving level. There are many fusion strategies (Wei & Liang, 2018). In the following part, we choose optimistic and pessimistic fusion strategies (Qian, Liang, Yao, & Dang, 2010; Qian, Zhang, Sang, & Liang, 2014; Qian, Liang, & Lin, 2017; Qian, Liu, & Yue, 2019) to fuse multiple views. Optimistic and pessimistic fusion strategies are proposed in multigranulation rough sets (MGRS) (Qian, Liang, Yao, & Dang, 2010), where the target concept is approximated through a family of indiscernibility relations. In the lower approximation (positive region), the word “optimistic” is used to express the idea that in multiple independent indiscernibility relations, we need only at least one of the indiscernibility relations to satisfy the inclusion condition between the equivalence class and the target concept, while the word “pessimistic” is used to express the idea that in multiple independent indiscernibility relations, we need all of the indiscernibility relations to satisfy the inclusion condition between the equivalence class and the target concept (Qian, Liang, Yao, & Dang, 2010; Qian, Zhang, Sang, & Liang, 2014; Qian, Liang, & Lin, 2017). Combining depth-first and breadth-first searching algorithms with optimistic and pessimistic fusion strategies, we propose four multiview sequential three-way decisions: depth-first optimistic multiview sequential three-way decisions, depth-first pessimistic multiview sequential three-way decisions, breadth-first optimistic multiview sequential three-way decisions, and breadth-first pessimistic multiview sequential three-way decisions.

The problem description space and problem solving space of multiview sequential three-way decisions based on partition order product space are shown in Fig.5. In Fig.5, according to Definition 3, the partition order product space consists of multiple views, and each view has multiple levels organized by linearly ordered relations. Therefore, in the problem description space of multiview sequential three-way decisions based on partition order product space, there are multiple rectangles formed by dotted lines, and each one denotes a view. In each view, there are multiple dots, and each dot denotes a level, where multiple levels are organized by linearly ordered relation. Through the Cartesian product of multiple linearly ordered relations, multiple views with multiple levels can be integrated into a lattice, which is the problem solving space of multiview sequential three-way decisions. Each element in the lattice is a problem solving level denoted as a rectangle. Each problem solving level is a family of one-level views, as shown in the circle formed by dotted lines.

Assume that L= {l1,l2,…,lt} is a traversal sequence of problem solving levels based on depth-first or breadth-first searching algorithms, is the k-th problem solving level, , and is the equivalence class of x∈U with respect to In the following section, we introduce four multiview sequential three-way decisions.

Figure 5. Problem description space and problem solving space of multiview sequential three-way decisions based on partition order product space

Depth-First Optimistic Multiview Sequential Three-Way Decisions

Based on the depth-first searching algorithm and optimistic fusion strategy, depth-first optimistic multiview sequential three-way decisions are defined as follows:

Definition 5. Let L= {l1,l2,…,lt} be a traversal sequence of problem solving levels based on depth-first searching algorithm, X⊆U be a target concept. Given m pairs of thresholds , the positive region, negative region and boundary region of the k-th problem solving level of depth-first optimistic multiview sequential three-way decisions are defined as:

Depth-first optimistic multiview sequential three-way decisions are the combination of the depth-first searching algorithm and optimistic fusion strategy. The depth-first searching algorithm obtains a sequence of problem solving levels to construct a sequential decision process. The optimistic fusion strategy fuses multiple one-level views at the problem solving level to make three-way decisions. At the problem solving level, according to the optimistic fusion strategy, in the positive region, we use the operation “disjunction” to fuse multiple views, which makes three-way decisions from multiview. Based on a sequence of problem solving levels, from the high problem solving level to the low problem solving level, we make three-way decisions from multilevel. Consequently, depth-first optimistic multiview sequential three-way decisions can make decisions not only from multiple different views but also at multiple abstract levels. We can flexibly change views and levels to make decisions more reasonable. The detailed process is described in Algorithm 3.

For breadth-first optimistic multiview sequential three-way decisions, the positive region is defined by ”disjunction” (Equation 14 of Definition 7), and the negative region is defined by ”conjunction” (Equation 15 of Definition 7). As shown in Example 5 and Example 6, compared with breadth-first optimistic multiview sequential three-way decisions, breadth-first pessimistic multiview sequential three-way decisions have fewer objects in the positive region and a larger number of objects in the negative region.

We summarize the advantages and limitations of the proposed multiview sequential three-way decisions. First, as partition order product space simultaneously provides the understanding and description of a problem from multiple views and multiple levels, the proposed four multiview sequential three-way decisions based on partition order product space can solve a problem not only from multiview but also from multilevel. The integration of multiview and multilevel renders the understanding and description of the problem more comprehensive and then solves the problem more effectively and reasonably. Second, note that for the proposed multiview sequential three-way decisions based on partition order product space, when the number of views is one and the number of levels in a view is one, the proposed models degenerate to classical three-way decisions. When the number of views is one, the proposed models degenerate to sequential three-way decisions. When the number of levels in each view is one, the proposed models degenerate to multigranulation three-way decisions. When the number of levels in each view is one and we use different thresholds on different granularity levels of the sequential process, the proposed models degenerate to multigranulation sequential three-way decisions. Therefore, existing three-way decisions can be considered special cases of the proposed multiview sequential three-way decisions. Last, the proposed multiview sequential three-way decisions also have limitations. With an increasing number of views and levels in each view, the complexity of the problem solving space of multiview sequential three-way decisions, which are based on partition order product space, will increase dramatically, resulting in a combinatorial explosion. Therefore, in future work, we will investigate the reduction method of the problem solving space to reduce the complexity of problem solving.

CONCLUSION

Granular computing exploits problem solving and information processing governed by a multiview principle and a multilevel principle. In order to understand and describe problem in a more comprehensive way, and then solve the problem more effectively and reasonably, we propose partition order product space. Partition order product space is a new granular computing model that follows the principles of multiview and multilevel. To obtain a solution for problem solving in partition order product space, we propose two search algorithms, which are referred to as the depth-first searching algorithm and breadth-first searching algorithm. We discuss three-way decisions based on the partition order product space. By combining depth-first and breadth-first searching algorithms with optimistic and pessimistic fusion strategies, we propose four multiview sequential three-way decisions, which can make decisions not only from multiple different views but also at multiple abstract levels. Existing three-way decisions may be considered special cases of the proposed models. Multiview sequential three-way decisions can make decision from multiview and multilevel to obtain more reasonable decision results, which can be used in intelligent medical, recommender system, management decision. In the future, we can investigate more effective methods to determine the evaluation functions and thresholds under multiview sequential three-way decisions based on partition order product space.

Chapter 6

  • Chunmao Jiang
    Fujian University of Technology, China

ABSTRACT

In this chapter, we enhance the trisecting-acting-outcome (TAO) model of three-way decision-making (3WD) with a novel approach for strategy selection and outcome prediction using Q-learning in reinforcement learning. We reinterpret the changes in tripartition and actions in the TAO model as states and actions in reinforcement learning, respectively. The reward is quantified using cumulative prospect theory, and the Q-learning algorithm iteratively determines action sets that achieve target rewards efficiently. This method offers a cost-effective and psychologically attuned action set for predicting the utility in change-based 3WD, demonstrated through a practical example.

INTRODUCTION

The three-way decision (3WD) model is consistent with human cognition and offers a nuanced semantic framework for understanding decision-making processes. This approach categorizes decisions into three distinct categories: acceptance, non-commitment, and rejection, each derived from the positive, boundary, and negative regions of rough set approximations, respectively (Yao, 2009). In 2012, Yao refined this concept, proposing a model that divides a universal set into three segments to facilitate more precise classifications (Yao, 2012).

Over time, the scope of 3WD has expanded beyond its original probabilistic rough set basis, evolving into a broader conceptual framework, to form a complex research network (Yang & Li, 2019). This more expansive interpretation of 3WD emphasizes a triadic approach to thought and problem solving, a method prevalent across various disciplines and supported by cognitive theory. This approach simplifies complex problems by dividing them into three interconnected but distinct components, reducing cognitive and information overload (Yao, 2019). In its evolution and development, a large number of research results were produced (Fang & Min, 2019; Liu & Liang, 2016; Li & Huang, 2017; Min & Zhu, 2012; Qian & Liu, 2020; Wang & Yao, 2018; Zhang & Li, 2020, Zhang & Pang, 2020; Yu & Wang, 2020; Yang & Li, 2019; Li & Huang, 2017; Zhan & Wang, 2023; Wang & Li, 2022; Wang & Ma, 2022).

A notable example of this expansive interpretation is the trisecting-acting-outcome (TAO) model, where ‘trisecting’ refers to dividing the universal set into three parts, and ‘acting’ is the process of selecting and providing the optimal action that fulfills the result and maintains them at a moderate level. On the one hand, based on the required outcome, the decision maker designed appropriate strategies for the tripartition to achieve the expected results. On the other hand, strategies are selected to maintain the outcome at a moderate level. The outcome refers to the effectiveness of the results of trisecting and acting.

Jiang and Yao (2018) introduced a quantitative evaluation method based on a general 3WD model, movement-based 3WD, and Jiang and Guo (2020) developed a probabilistic model for strategy selection based on information entropy. They also introduced the proportional utility function (PUF) for assessing outcomes from dual perspectives in movement-based 3WD (Jiang & Guo, 2021; Jiang & Guo, 2022). In addition, the change-based TAO model (Jiang & Duan, 2022) was proposed to measure effectiveness by integrating interval sets and distinctive utility functions. This framework uses interval sets to represent the impact of strategies or actions, using a utility measurement method to assess changes in three intervals and amalgamating these utilities for a comprehensive effectiveness evaluation.

However, some key issues still need to be adequately addressed when dealing with change-based three-way decisions. The goal of a change-based three-way decision is to change the object from the original tripartition to a more effective one. The three-way decision based on changes explains and answers one type of question: Why do we need to ‘Trisecting and Acting’? That is, the three-way decision is intended to produce more satisfactory changes. In this chapter, we develop a method for selecting optimal strategies and calculating future utility based on change-based three-way decisions.

This chapter applies reinforcement learning to predict future utilities and generate a set of strategies to reach the target reward in the shortest cycle during future utility computation using the Q-learning algorithm. During the prediction process, altered tripartition can be treated as states in reinforcement learning. Multiple strategies for applying to the altered tripartition are available and these strategies are referred to as actions in reinforcement learning. Each time the strategy has changed the tripartition, it has produced a utility referred to as a reward for reinforcement learning.

The Motives and Contribution of This Chapter

The primary motivation behind this research is to address critical issues in change-based three-way decisions (C-3WD) and to improve the understanding of the Trisecting-Acting-Outcome (TAO) model in decision-making. While previous studies have mainly focused on the ‘trisecting’ and ‘Acting’ phases, little attention has been given to the ‘outcome.’ Additionally, there is a need to find strategies that can achieve desired utility efficiently in a finite cycle, reducing trial-and-error costs.

To address these challenges, this research proposes a method that leverages reinforcement learning to predict future utilities and generate optimal strategies for change-based three-way decisions. Key contributions of this work include the following:

  • 1. Focus on change-based three-way decisions: The research shifts its focus to change-based three-way decisions (C-3WD), which aim to transform the original tripartition into a more effective one. This addresses why ‘Trisecting and Acting’ must produce more satisfactory changes.
  • 2. Reinforcement Learning Approach: The proposed method, specifically the Q-learning algorithm, utilizes reinforcement learning to predict future utilities and select strategies. Changed tripartitions are treated as states and strategies for tripartition changes are regarded as actions. The aim is to achieve the target reward efficiently in the shortest cycle.
  • 3. Outcome Prediction-Based Strategy Selection: This research contributes to the field of three-way decision-making by addressing issues in change-based three-way decisions and providing a novel approach to strategy selection and outcome evaluation using reinforcement learning. The goal is to find the best match between trading and acting in terms of effectiveness, efficiency, and interpretability.

According to the above analysis, we arranged the structure of this chapter below. Section 2 reviews the fundamental concepts of change-based three-way decisions and reinforcement learning. Section 3 describes specifically the method of strategy selection and outcome evaluation for change-based three-way decisions using reinforcement learning. Section 4 provides an illustrative example to demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, and Section 5 concludes the chapter with suggestions for future research directions.

BASIC KNOWLEDGE

TAO Model

Figure 1 illustrates the comprehensive processes of the Trisecting-Acting-Outcome (TAO) model in three-way decision making (Yao, 2020). This model comprises three interconnected components: trisecting, acting, and outcome, each with distinct but related functions. The TAO model not only delineates the individual roles of these components but also elucidates their interdependencies. While each part operates independently, they collectively form a cohesive whole and are either distinctly separate or weakly joined.

Trisecting is a crucial step in the three-way decision process, significantly influencing the overall outcome. Its effectiveness lies in its ability to produce varied results based on the method of trisection used, underscoring its role as a fundamental mechanism in achieving a successful trisection, a core concept in three-way decision making.

Acting is another vital aspect of the TAO framework. It involves applying specific strategies to the three-segmented parts to meet predefined objectives. The effectiveness of the three-way decision is highly dependent on the acting step, as different strategies yield different outcomes, affecting the decision-making process’s overall efficacy.

Both trisecting and acting are instrumental in determining the success of three-way decisions: the application of the TAO model, whether trisection-driven or action-driven, varies depending on the context. The trisection-driven approach emphasizes optimizing trisecting methods, with subsequent actions and strategies developed based on the trisection results. Conversely, the action-driven approach prioritizes strategy selection from a given set to influence the three-way decision's effectiveness, determining how to divide a whole into three regions best. Often, these two approaches are integrated to enhance the applicability and effectiveness of the three-way decision in various scenarios.

The outcome evaluation component is distinct from trisecting and acting, focusing primarily on assessing the effectiveness of these two processes. Considers the results of both the trisection and the strategies employed, providing valuable feedback that informs future decisions and strategy adjustments. This evaluative step is essential to measure the overall impact and success of the three-way decision-making process.

Evaluation of Outcome

The primary function of the outcome in three-way decision making is to assess the process’s effectiveness. This assessment focuses on identifying and analyzing the differences that emerge before and after implementing the trisecting and acting steps. To quantify this change, we use the following general formula (Gao & Yao, 2017):

In this equation, Q(π) and Q(π’) denote the initial and subsequent quantified outcomes, respectively. This measurement can evaluate aspects such as benefit, cost, or utility. While a direct calculation of Q(π) and Q(π’) might not always be feasible, this formula still offers a means to gauge the difference. Occasionally, the measure Q(π’|π) can be assessed from alternative perspectives.

In existing research, much emphasis is placed on the aspects of tripartition and action, with limited focus on outcome evaluation. Yao and Jiang, in their pioneering work, proposed a comprehensive metric framework for measuring outcomes based on Trisecting and Acting, as indicated in the following equation:

Here, Q(π) signifies the overall results, which may encompass cost, benefit, or risk. Q(Pi), i=1,2,3 represents the outcome of a specific region Pi, and wi is the weight assigned to Q(Pi), i=1,2,3. This framework facilitates a more nuanced and comprehensive evaluation of the outcomes, contributing significantly to the field of three-way decision-making.

Change-Based Three-Way Decisions

Definition 8.1: (Jiang et al., 2022). An evaluation space is defined by a triplet E=(U,S,e), where U is a finite non-empty set of objects, S is a set of states, and e is an evaluation from U×S to the set of real number , namely, . For a pair of an object x∈U and a state s∈S, e(xs) denotes the evaluation value of x in state s.

As a special case of , we may use a three-valued set {-1,0,+1} to qualitatively indicate some properties of objects. We may also use the unit interval [0,1]. The evaluation value e(xs) represents the object in states. By looking at the two states, we can observe changes.

Definition 8.2: (Jiang et al., 2022). In an evaluation space E(U,S,e), given a pair of states , the change of evaluation values of an object x∈U is defined by:

In the definition above, we produce a new evaluation method. It does not merely evaluate an object in one state, and it uses the object’s values in two different states by calculating their difference. The new evaluation extends the traditional evaluation methods. More specifically, we employ the difference between two values as changes. It does not relate this difference to the initial value e(xs). Sometimes it needs to consider changes relative to the value e(xs).

In some situations, we may want to evaluate the overall changes of a set of objects. The simplest way is to summarize the changes of the objects in the set.

The summation collects the differences of all objects in the set X in two states. If the summation result is over zero, the strategy achieves a positive effect; if the result is zero, there is no change; otherwise, the approach will offer a negative effect, so the summation can provide a qualitative characterization for a strategy.

Reinforcement Learning

Reinforcement Learning (RL) (Kaelbling, 1996), denoted as a method in machine learning, emphasizes how agents learn the optimal strategy in an environment through their actions and the feedback from rewards received. Assuming that the environment possesses Markovian characteristics, sequential reinforcement learning problems can be aptly modeled through Markov Decision Processes (MDPs).

The change of trisecting states by strategy acting adheres to Markovian properties, meaning that the subsequent trisecting state solely depends on the current state and policy, irrespective of history. A Markov Decision Process is represented by the tuple πc, A,P,R>. Here, πc is a finite set encompassing all possible trisecting states, while A is a finite set of all applicable strategies. P represents the probability of transition to the next state transition probability , indicating the likelihood of transitioning to the next state under the current state πc and strategy A. The reward function quantifies the reward obtained for transitioning to state under the conditions of state πc and strategy A. Owing to its capacity to effectively encapsulate the dynamic interaction between an agent and its environment, MDPs are commonly used to describe reinforcement learning tasks.

The Q-learning algorithm in reinforcement learning seeks the optimal strategy in a Markov Decision Process (MDP) context by continuously updating a Q-table through exploration and learning. This table records the value function for each pair of state-actions, representing the expected return from executing a specific action. The algorithm updates the Q-function Q(πc,A) using the formula:

The balance between exploration and exploitation is managed by strategies like ε-greedy. This Q-learning approach, applied to 3WD, models the evolution of trisecting states under different strategies, optimizing strategy selection based on state dynamics. The algorithm aims to converge the Q-table towards the optimal value function, enabling the best action selection in any given state.

In this chapter, we define utility generated from changes in trisecting states as rewards, denoted as , where πc and are the current and subsequent trisecting states, and A is the applied strategy. The Q-function, Q(πc,A), updated with these rewards, guides strategy selection to maximize cumulative rewards. We introduce a target reward value, Rtarget, and consider exploration complete when the sum of rewards from sequential strategies reaches Rtarget. The process iterates until a stable and efficient strategy path emerges, as indicated by consistent attainment of Rtarget in the fewest cycles.

Integrating reinforcement learning with the study of changes in 3WD, the utility generated by the fluctuation in trisecting states can be utilized as rewards. These rewards serve to calculate and update the Q-function. Decisions are then made based on the Q-function to select strategies that maximize cumulative rewards. Given the ongoing changes in trisecting states under various strategies, this chapter proposes setting a target reward value. The exploration is deemed complete when the cumulative rewards generated by the changes in trisecting states under consecutive strategies reach this target value. Following this methodology, multiple explorations are conducted until a stable and shortest strategy path is consistently identified.

STRATEGY SELECTION AND UTILITY MEASUREMENT BASED ON REINFORCEMENT LEARNING

This section employs the Markov Decision Process to model maximizing utility through continuous optimization of strategy selection in changing trisecting states. Initially, quadratic programming is used to solve for state transition probabilities. Subsequently, the rewards generated by state changes are calculated using the cumulative prospect theory. Finally, the Q-learning algorithm is employed to identify the strategy that maximizes rewards in each cycle.

Figure 2. Three-way decision based on reinforcement learning (RL-3WD)

Figure 2 illustrates the process of updating the Q table using the Q-learning algorithm. For a trisecting state in cycle t, a strategy A is chosen using the ε-greedy approach, which, when applied, yields a more effective trisecting state in cycle t+1, thus generating a reward rt. This reward is then used to update the Q-table. This process is repeated through multiple training iterations until the Q-values in the Q-table stabilize. The following outlines the specific approach for a series of strategy trainings on the trisecting states {R+,R0,R-}:

State Transition Probability Matrix: Calculate the transition probability matrix resulting from the application of each strategy. Based on this matrix, determine the trisecting states for the next cycle.

Use cumulative prospect theory to calculate the utility value of the new trisecting state generated by each strategy application and consider this as a reward in reinforcement learning.

Strategy Selection: Choose the strategy for each trisecting state in each cycle from the Q table using the ε-greedy approach.

Set Training Termination Criteria: Establish a target reward value during strategy training. Training stops when the cumulative reward of the training reaches this target value.

Conduct multiple trainings until the Q values in the Q-table stabilize, then select the strategy with the highest Q value for each cycle.

States and Transition Probability Matrix

In the Markov Decision Process related to three-way changes, the sequence of trisecting states that vary with cycles is considered as the state set. The application of different strategies yields various state-transition probability matrices. These matrices determine the distribution of trisecting states in the next cycle. This section employs quadratic programming to solve for the state transition probability matrix between different cycles.

Strategy Selection

For each change-based tripartition state in every cycle, there exist multiple strategies that can be applied, which are considered as the action set in the Markov Decision Process. The objective is to select a strategy that maximizes the cumulative reward from the initial to the terminal state of the change-based tripartition state. To achieve this, we employ the Q-learning algorithm, which continuously explores and learns to update a Q-table. This table records the value function of each pair of state-actions.

In the process of strategy selection, a Q-table is initially constructed with column labels as change-based tripartition states and row labels as applicable strategies Ai. At the beginning of the cycle, all values in the Q-table are initialized to zero. For the change-based tripartition state corresponding to the cycle in the Q-table, a -greedy strategy is used to choose the strategy to apply. Specifically, when the action value function Q(πc,A) is greater than ε or all Q(πc,A) values are zero, a strategy is randomly selected for implementation. Otherwise, the strategy corresponding to the maximum value Q(πc,A) in that cycle is chosen.

The values of Q(πc,A) in the Q-table are continuously updated. The specific formula for updating Q(πc,A) is as follows. Suppose strategy Am is applied to the change based tripartition state of cycle i, then the real calculation formula for is

According to Algorithm 1, an updated Q-table can be obtained. The strategy with the highest Q value for each change-based tripartition state in the updated Q-table can be selected to form an optimal strategy sequence to achieve the target reward in the shortest time. This sequence of strategies, learned from experience, represents the strategies that can achieve maximum utility, thus guiding future strategy selection.

Reward and Future Utility

In the Markov Decision Process of three-way decision making, each change in the change-based tripartition state generates a reward to update the Q-table. We employ the cumulative prospect theory to calculate the rewards generated in each cycle.

Cumulative prospect theory describes decision-makers’ behavior and attitudes toward risk under conditions of uncertainty and risk. Its principal ideas can be summarized in three aspects: Outcomes are viewed as gains or losses relative to a reference point, rather than as final states of wealth. Second, decision-makers exhibit risk aversion for gains, and risk-seeking for losses, and are more sensitive to losses than gains. Lastly, in the face of low-probability events, decision-makers tend to magnify their impact, while for high-probability events, they tend to downplay it. The Cumulative Prospect Theory suggests that decision-makers prefer decisions with the highest cumulative prospect value. Using the value function v(xh) and the decision weight function ψh, the cumulative prospect value function v is given by:

The rewards generated in each cycle during every training process can be determined based on calculated rewards, thereby estimating the future utility of three-way decision changes. The Q-learning algorithm is used to update the Q-table and to identify the shortest path to the target reward through a sequence of strategies based on the Q-table. Combined with the state transition probability matrix, a future sequence of change-based tripartition states can be predicted, and the reward for each cycle is calculated using cumulative prospect theory. Since this method employs cumulative prospect theory to calculate rewards generated in each cycle for predicting future utility, it more accurately reflects the decision-maker’s behavioral preferences. Future utility calculated using this method can estimate outcomes before a series of strategies are executed and provide relatively accurate predictions.

As delineated in this paper, the three-way decision framework employing reinforcement learning offers an innovative approach to optimizing strategy selection and enhancing utility measurement. The application of reinforcement learning to the three-way decision method enables the maximization of cumulative rewards, demonstrating a significant stride in decision-making methodologies. Nevertheless, this approach presents opportunities for further refinement. Presently, the state transition matrix relies on quadratic programming for its resolution. This aspect could be more efficiently addressed by employing advanced algorithms, such as policy gradient methods inherent in deep reinforcement learning. Moreover, incorporating affective computing into the reward calculation could align the reward function more closely with the decision-maker's preferences, thereby enhancing the model's applicability and accuracy.

While integrating reinforcement learning into the three-way decision framework marks a theoretical advancement, its practical application is still nascent and warrants extensive exploration. Future research should pivot towards applying this model in concrete scenarios, such as medical decision-making or financial investment decisions. This application-oriented approach would involve collecting real-world data and establishing Markov process models specific to the problem at hand. Utilizing the proposed method in these real-life scenarios would validate its effectiveness in practical settings and develop it into a reliable tool for supporting three-way decisions. Empirical analyses stemming from these applications could provide critical insights, thereby enabling further refinement of the method. This evolution would substantially augment its ability to address complex decision problems effectively.

Illustrative Example

This section illustrates the concept of this study using an example of a store operation. The objective here is to select a strategy that enables the store to reach the target reward in the shortest possible time within a limited number of cycles and to predict the store’s future revenue under the current state.

The operators regularly conduct various promotions on the platform to increase sales. Depending on the nature of the promotions, the sales volume of the products in the store can change to varying degrees. Based on the change in product sales volume, if the sales increase of a product exceeds 10, it is classified as a hot selling item; if the sales decrease by 10, it is classified as a potential item; otherwise, it is considered a promotional item, represented by R+, R-, and R0, respectively. The process of changing product sales in the store with each planned promotion is considered a cycle, typically lasting 3-5 days.

Currently, there are three traffic-driving activities a1, a2, a3 on the platform. For products in the store, appropriate traffic-driving activities are applied to the three different areas R+, R0, R-. The combination of activities applied to the three areas in each cycle is considered a strategy, and the product sales in the store change differently depending on the strategy implemented. Based on experience, three sets of strategies are now set: A1={a1,a3,a2}, A2={a3,a1,a2}, A3={a2,a2,a1}.

The method proposed in this chapter can better assist stores in strategy selection and utility assessment, guiding operators to better manage and run their stores, achieve profit maximization, and enhance market share and competitiveness, thus holding substantial practical significance.

CONCLUSION

This chapter discusses the ‘Acting’ and ‘efficiency’ within the TAO model of change-based three-way decision making, introducing reinforcement learning into strategy selection and utility measurement of change-based three-way decisions. Utilizing Cumulative Prospect Theory, it calculates the rewards generated by state transitions in each cycle and uses these as feedback signals. The Q-learning algorithm is then used to update the Q-table, from which the shortest sequence of strategies to reach the target reward is selected and future utility is predicted.

The introduction of reinforcement learning into the three-way the model enhances decision efficiency and quality of the decision, offering novel and effective solutions for other types of decision models. However, this chapter also has some limitations, such as not considering the issue of changing thresholds for trisecting regions with environmental changes and not describing methods to adjust the parameters of the Q-learning algorithm according to specific problems and environments. Future research will further explore these areas.
